## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

20	   - **`/prototype`** to answer the question with throwaway code,
21	   - **`/handoff`** back what you learned, and reference it from the original idea thread.

23	   - **Yes** → **`/to-spec`** (turn the thread into a spec), then **`/to-tickets`** to split it into tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its **blocking edges**. On a local tracker that's an ordered `tickets.md` you work by hand; on a real tracker the edges become native blocking links, so any ticket whose blockers are done can be grabbed — kick off **`/implement`** per ticket, **clearing context between each one**.
24	   - **No** → **`/implement`** right here, in the same context window.
25	
26	   Either way, **`/implement`** builds each issue by driving **`/tdd`** internally — one red-green slice at a time — then closes out by running **`/code-review`**, a two-axis review (Standards + Spec) of the diff, before committing. Reach for **`/tdd`** on its own when you just want to build a concrete behaviour test-first without a full spec, and **`/code-review`** on its own whenever you want to review a branch or PR against a fixed point.
27	
28	### Context hygiene
29	
30	Keep steps 1–3 in **one unbroken context window** — don't compact or clear until after `/to-tickets` — so the grilling, spec, and tickets all build on the same thinking. Each `/implement` then starts fresh, working from the ticket.
31	
32	The limit on this is the **[smart zone](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/smart-zone)**: the window (~120k tokens on state-of-the-art models) within which the model still reasons sharply. If a session approaches it before `/to-tickets`, don't push on degraded — `/handoff` and continue in a fresh thread.
33	
34	## On-ramps
35	
36	A starting situation that generates work, then merges onto the main flow.
37	
38	- **Bugs and requests piling up** → **`/triage`**. It moves issues through triage roles and produces agent-ready issues, which **`/implement`** later picks up.
39	
40	  Triage is only for issues **you didn't create** — bug reports, incoming feature requests, anything that arrives raw. Tickets that `/to-tickets` produced are already agent-ready, so **don't triage them**.
41	
42	- **Something's broken** → **`/diagnosing-bugs`**. For the hard ones: the bug that resists a first glance, the intermittent flake, the regression that crept in between two known-good states. It refuses to theorise until it has a **tight feedback loop** — one command that already goes red on *this* bug — then fixes with a regression test. Its post-mortem hands off to **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** when the real finding is that there's no good seam to lock the bug down.
43	
44	- **A huge, foggy effort — a greenfield project or a huge feature build, too big for one session** → **`/wayfinder`**. When the way from here to the destination isn't visible yet, it charts a **shared map** of investigation tickets on the issue tracker and resolves them one at a time — producing **decisions, not deliverables** — until the fog is pushed back and the way is clear. Then it merges onto the main flow at **`/to-spec`** (or, if the effort turned out small enough, straight to **`/implement`**). Where **`/grill-with-docs`** sharpens an idea you can hold in one session, wayfinder is for the idea you can't.
45	
46	## Codebase health
47	
48	Not feature work — upkeep.
49	
50	- **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** — run whenever you have a spare moment to keep the codebase good for agents to operate in. It surfaces **deepening opportunities**; picking one _generates an idea_ you can take into the main flow at `/grill-with-docs`. It's the survey that finds the candidates; **`/codebase-design`** (below) is the bench you design the chosen one on.
51	
52	## Vocabulary underneath
53	
54	Two model-invoked references that run *beneath* the other skills — each the single source of truth for its vocabulary. Reach for them directly when the **words**, not the process, are the problem; or let the skills above pull them in.
55	
56	- **`/domain-modeling`** — sharpen the project's *domain* language: challenge a fuzzy term, resolve an overloaded word ("account" doing three jobs), record a hard-to-reverse decision as an ADR. It's the active discipline `/grill-with-docs` drives to keep `CONTEXT.md` a clean glossary.
57	- **`/codebase-design`** — the deep-module vocabulary (module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality) for designing a module's *shape*: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface at a clean seam. `/tdd` and `/improve-codebase-architecture` both speak it.
58	
59	## Crossing sessions
60	
61	- **`/handoff`** — when a thread is full or you need to branch off (e.g. into a `/prototype` session), this compacts the conversation into a markdown file. You don't continue in place — you **open a new session and reference that file** to carry the context across. It's the bridge between context windows, in either direction. Use it when you want a **fresh session** but need the **current conversation preserved**.
62	- **`/compact`** (built-in) — stay in the **same conversation**, letting the earlier turns be summarized. Use it at **intentional breaks between phases**, when you don't mind losing the verbatim history. Don't compact mid-phase — the agent can lose its way. `/handoff` forks; `/compact` continues.
63	
64	## Standalone
65	
66	Off the main flow entirely.
67	
68	- **`/grill-me`** — the same relentless interview as `/grill-with-docs`, but for when you have **no codebase**. Stateless: it saves nothing locally, builds no `CONTEXT.md`. Reach for it to sharpen any plan or design that doesn't live in a repo.
69	- **`/prototype`** — a small, throwaway program that answers one design question: does this state model feel right, or what should this UI look like. Throwaway from day one — keep the answer, delete the code. It's the detour in step 2 of the main flow, but reach for it any time a design question is hard to settle on paper.
70	- **`/research`** — delegate reading legwork to a **background agent**: it investigates a question against **primary sources**, then leaves a cited Markdown file in the repo. Keep working while it reads. The file it produces is something to take *into* the main flow at `/grill-with-docs` — research feeds the thinking, it doesn't replace it.
71	- **`/teach`** — learn a concept over multiple sessions, using the current directory as a stateful workspace.
72	- **`/writing-great-skills`** — reference for writing and editing skills well.
73	
74	## Precondition
75	
76	**`/setup-matt-pocock-skills`** — run before your first engineering flow to configure the issue tracker, triage labels, and doc layout the other skills assume. Custom issue trackers also work.

Off the main flow entirely.

- **`/grill-me`** — the same relentless interview as `/grill-with-docs`, but for when you have **no codebase**. Stateless: it saves nothing locally, builds no `CONTEXT.md`. Reach for it to sharpen any plan or design that doesn't live in a repo.
- **`/prototype`** — a small, throwaway program that answers one design question: does this state model feel right, or what should this UI look like. Throwaway from day one — keep the answer, delete the code. It's the detour in step 2 of the main flow, but reach for it any time a design question is hard to settle on paper.
- **`/research`** — delegate reading legwork to a **background agent**: it investigates a question against **primary sources**, then leaves a cited Markdown file in the repo. Keep working while it reads. The file it produces is something to take *into* the main flow at `/grill-with-docs` — research feeds the thinking, it doesn't replace it.
- **`/teach`** — learn a concept over multiple sessions, using the current directory as a stateful workspace.
- **`/writing-great-skills`** — reference for writing and editing skills well.

## Precondition

**`/setup-matt-pocock-skills`** — run before your first engineering flow to configure the issue tracker, triage labels, and doc layout the other skills assume. Custom issue trackers also work.

# S2_Evaluation — recommended workflow

**Project:** Mine existing S2 Cognition testing data for actionable, coach-facing
insights that go beyond normative percentiles.
**Lane:** side · **Stage:** idea · **Registered:** 2026-08-08
**Routed via:** `/ask-matt` (router doc at `~/.agents/skills/ask-matt/SKILL.md`)

---

## The framing problem to solve first

The request as stated — "mine the data for insights" — is open-ended exploration
with no decision anchor. That is the single biggest risk to this project, and your
own material already says so:

- Your vault's graphify report (Community 2) records the lesson
  **"Data Collection Without Clear Plan = Unutilized Info"** and a
  **"Decision-First Data Collection Approach."**
- Robertson et al. 2017 in your library argues athlete monitoring fails without
  *decision-support systems* — more numbers is not the fix.

"Beyond percentiles" is a real goal, but an insight that isn't tied to a decision a
coach actually makes is just a prettier percentile. **Step 1 is framing, not
analysis.**

Concretely, the grilling should force answers to: *which coaching decisions should
an S2 insight change?* Candidates worth pressuring — install/rep allocation,
position fit, communication load in complex packages, individualized coaching cues,
pre-snap processing under time pressure. Pick the few that a coach would act on.

---

## Recommended path

### 0. Precondition (gate, not a step)
`/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configures the issue tracker, triage labels, and doc
layout the later steps assume. **No Matt tracker config was found on this machine.**
It is not needed for steps 1–3. Run it only if you reach step 4 (`/to-tickets`).

### 1. `/grill-with-docs` — sharpen the idea, statefully
Run this in `S2_Evaluation/`. Purpose: nail the decision-first frame above, and
build the glossary.

Strictly, `/ask-matt` routes an empty folder to `/grill-me` (no codebase). Use
`/grill-with-docs` anyway — `/grill-me` is **stateless and saves nothing**, and
this project will accumulate decisions worth a paper trail (`CONTEXT.md` + ADRs).
Precedent: `SportScienceResearchRepo`, `ZoteroInjestion`, and `PlayerProfiles_FB`
all carry a `CONTEXT.md` from this flow.

Expect `/domain-modeling` to get pulled in underneath: **"S2 score" is an
overloaded term** doing at least four jobs — raw subtest value, subtest percentile,
composite, and normative-population percentile. Resolving that is a prerequisite to
saying anything precise about "beyond percentiles."

### 2. `/research` — run in the background, in parallel with step 1
Delegate to a background agent, against **primary sources**: what each S2 subtest
actually claims to measure, and the published evidence on predictive validity for
on-field performance. It leaves a cited Markdown file in the repo.

This is not optional politeness. If you mine a pattern that contradicts the
instrument's known construct validity, you will present it to a coach and be wrong.
Pair with your own `sports-science-research-grounding` and
`pp-zotero-research-library` skills.

### 3. `/prototype` — answer "is there signal?" with throwaway code
The question *"is there anything beyond percentiles in this data?"* cannot be
settled on paper. It needs a runnable answer, which is exactly the step-2 detour in
the main flow.

`/prototype` fits exploratory data analysis almost perfectly: **throwaway from day
one — keep the answer, delete the code.** Probe intra-athlete profile *shape*
(strength/weakness dispersion, not rank), change across testing cycles,
position-relevant subtest weighting, and subtest interactions.

Bridge with `/handoff` in both directions — out of the grilling session into a
fresh prototype session, then back with what you learned.

### 4. Branch — only after step 3 finds signal
- **Multi-session build** (likely, if this becomes a recurring per-testing-cycle
  deliverable) → `/to-spec`, then `/to-tickets`, then `/implement` per ticket,
  **clearing context between each one**.
- **Small enough** → `/implement` directly.

`/implement` drives `/tdd` internally and closes with `/code-review` before
committing.

**Context hygiene:** keep steps 1–4 through `/to-tickets` in one unbroken context
window. If you approach the smart zone (~120k tokens) first, `/handoff` rather than
push on degraded.

---

## The last mile `/ask-matt` does not cover

`/ask-matt` routes **engineering** work. Your actual deliverable is **coach-facing**,
which is a data-storytelling problem, not a code problem. Once you have findings:

- **`design-academy-skill`** — audience-first data storytelling; it triggers exactly
  on "showing data to an audience."
- **`dataviz`** — read *before* writing the first line of chart code.
- **`five-slides-generator`** — if the output should land in the Performance School
  "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" format.

---

## Explicitly not recommended

- **`/triage`** — only for issues *you didn't create*. Nothing inbound here.
- **`/diagnosing-bugs`** — nothing is broken.
- **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** — no codebase yet.
- **`/wayfinder`** — the escalation, not the start. It charts investigation tickets
  for efforts too big for one session. Reach for it only if step 1 reveals the fog
  is deeper than a single grilling session; with data already in hand, grill +
  prototype is right-sized for a side-lane project.

---

## Immediate next action

Run `/grill-with-docs` in `S2_Evaluation/` to fix the decision-first frame — name
the specific coaching decisions an S2 insight should change, before touching the
data. Kick off `/research` in the background at the same time.

**Still unknown:** where the S2 Cognition data actually lives, its format, athlete
count, and how many testing cycles deep it goes. The grilling should surface this
early — it bounds what step 3 can attempt.

# S2_Evaluation — recommended workflow

**Project:** Mine existing S2 Cognition testing data for actionable, coach-facing
insights that go beyond normative percentiles.
**Lane:** side · **Stage:** idea · **Registered:** 2026-08-08
**Routed via:** `/ask-matt` (router doc at `~/.agents/skills/ask-matt/SKILL.md`)

---

## The framing problem to solve first

The request as stated — "mine the data for insights" — is open-ended exploration
with no decision anchor. That is the single biggest risk to this project, and your
own material already says so:

- Your vault's graphify report (Community 2) records the lesson
  **"Data Collection Without Clear Plan = Unutilized Info"** and a
  **"Decision-First Data Collection Approach."**
- Robertson et al. 2017 in your library argues athlete monitoring fails without
  *decision-support systems* — more numbers is not the fix.

"Beyond percentiles" is a real goal, but an insight that isn't tied to a decision a
coach actually makes is just a prettier percentile. **Step 1 is framing, not
analysis.**

Concretely, the grilling should force answers to: *which coaching decisions should
an S2 insight change?* Candidates worth pressuring — install/rep allocation,
position fit, communication load in complex packages, individualized coaching cues,
pre-snap processing under time pressure. Pick the few that a coach would act on.

---

## Recommended path

### 0. Precondition (gate, not a step)
`/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configures the issue tracker, triage labels, and doc
layout the later steps assume. **No Matt tracker config was found on this machine.**
It is not needed for steps 1–3. Run it only if you reach step 4 (`/to-tickets`).

### 1. `/grill-with-docs` — sharpen the idea, statefully
Run this in `S2_Evaluation/`. Purpose: nail the decision-first frame above, and
build the glossary.

Strictly, `/ask-matt` routes an empty folder to `/grill-me` (no codebase). Use
`/grill-with-docs` anyway — `/grill-me` is **stateless and saves nothing**, and
this project will accumulate decisions worth a paper trail (`CONTEXT.md` + ADRs).
Precedent: `SportScienceResearchRepo`, `ZoteroInjestion`, and `PlayerProfiles_FB`
all carry a `CONTEXT.md` from this flow.

Expect `/domain-modeling` to get pulled in underneath: **"S2 score" is an
overloaded term** doing at least four jobs — raw subtest value, subtest percentile,
composite, and normative-population percentile. Resolving that is a prerequisite to
saying anything precise about "beyond percentiles."

### 2. `/research` — run in the background, in parallel with step 1
Delegate to a background agent, against **primary sources**: what each S2 subtest
actually claims to measure, and the published evidence on predictive validity for
on-field performance. It leaves a cited Markdown file in the repo.

This is not optional politeness. If you mine a pattern that contradicts the
instrument's known construct validity, you will present it to a coach and be wrong.
Pair with your own `sports-science-research-grounding` and
`pp-zotero-research-library` skills.

### 3. `/prototype` — answer "is there signal?" with throwaway code
The question *"is there anything beyond percentiles in this data?"* cannot be
settled on paper. It needs a runnable answer, which is exactly the step-2 detour in
the main flow.

`/prototype` fits exploratory data analysis almost perfectly: **throwaway from day
one — keep the answer, delete the code.** Probe intra-athlete profile *shape*
(strength/weakness dispersion, not rank), change across testing cycles,
position-relevant subtest weighting, and subtest interactions.

Bridge with `/handoff` in both directions — out of the grilling session into a
fresh prototype session, then back with what you learned.

### 4. Branch — only after step 3 finds signal
- **Multi-session build** (likely, if this becomes a recurring per-testing-cycle
  deliverable) → `/to-spec`, then `/to-tickets`, then `/implement` per ticket,
  **clearing context between each one**.
- **Small enough** → `/implement` directly.

`/implement` drives `/tdd` internally and closes with `/code-review` before
committing.

**Context hygiene:** keep steps 1–4 through `/to-tickets` in one unbroken context
window. If you approach the smart zone (~120k tokens) first, `/handoff` rather than
push on degraded.

---

## The last mile `/ask-matt` does not cover

`/ask-matt` routes **engineering** work. Your actual deliverable is **coach-facing**,
which is a data-storytelling problem, not a code problem. Once you have findings:

- **`design-academy-skill`** — audience-first data storytelling; it triggers exactly
  on "showing data to an audience."
- **`dataviz`** — read *before* writing the first line of chart code.
- **`five-slides-generator`** — if the output should land in the Performance School
  "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" format.

---

## Explicitly not recommended

- **`/triage`** — only for issues *you didn't create*. Nothing inbound here.
- **`/diagnosing-bugs`** — nothing is broken.
- **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** — no codebase yet.
- **`/wayfinder`** — the escalation, not the start. It charts investigation tickets
  for efforts too big for one session. Reach for it only if step 1 reveals the fog
  is deeper than a single grilling session; with data already in hand, grill +
  prototype is right-sized for a side-lane project.

---

## Immediate next action

Run `/grill-with-docs` in `S2_Evaluation/` to fix the decision-first frame — name
the specific coaching decisions an S2 insight should change, before touching the
data. Kick off `/research` in the background at the same time.

**Still unknown:** where the S2 Cognition data actually lives, its format, athlete
count, and how many testing cycles deep it goes. The grilling should surface this
early — it bounds what step 3 can attempt.

/* ── broadcast masthead ──────────────────────────────────── */
.topline { height: 4px; background: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--gold) 0 62%, var(--green) 62% 100%); }
header { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center;

h1 { font-family: "Oswald", "Arial Narrow", ui-sans-serif, sans-serif;

  margin: 0; color: var(--chalk); }
h1 .gold { color: var(--gold); }
.sub { display: flex; gap: 8px; align-items: center; font-family: "Oswald", "Arial Narrow", sans-serif;

/* ── the bug (front burner) ──────────────────────────────── */
.hero { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 0; background: var(--bug);

.hero-card { padding: 20px 24px 16px; display: flex; flex-direction: column;
  align-items: flex-start; position: relative; min-width: 0; }
.hero-card + .hero-card { border-left: 1px solid var(--bug-edge); }

.hero-card > * { width: 100%; }
.lane-label { width: auto !important; font-family: "Oswald", "Arial Narrow", sans-serif;

.hero-card .update { color: var(--mist-faint); font-size: 12px; margin-top: 3px;

.hero-card .last-touch { color: var(--mist-faint); font-size: 12px; margin-top: auto;
  padding-top: 12px; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }

/* up-next ribbon */
.hero-secondary { display: grid; grid-template-columns: auto 1fr 1fr; gap: 14px;
  align-items: center; margin-top: 10px; padding: 9px 16px; background: var(--bug);
  border: 1px solid var(--bug-edge); border-radius: 6px; }
.hero-secondary::before { content: "UP NEXT"; font-family: "Oswald", "Arial Narrow", sans-serif;
  font-size: 11px; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 0.14em; color: var(--gold); }
.hero-secondary .mini-card { display: flex; align-items: baseline; gap: 9px;

.hero-secondary .mini-card .name { font-family: "Oswald", "Arial Narrow", sans-serif;

---
name: domain-modeling
description: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
---

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline — challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill — that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── CONTEXT.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily — only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y — which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account' — do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"

### Update CONTEXT.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up — capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

Here's my answer: **yes, proceed — neither blocker actually blocks.**

**The setup skill genuinely isn't needed.** I verified rather than assumed: `/grilling` is a pure interview with zero preconditions, and `/domain-modeling` creates `CONTEXT.md` and `docs/adr/` lazily. `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configures an issue tracker and labels for `/to-tickets` — that's step 4, and it's conditional on the prototype finding signal. Running it now would be setup for a step you may never take.

**The data being absent is the right condition, not a problem.** The entire decision-first premise is that you name the coaching decisions before looking at columns. Having the CSV open during grilling is a mild hazard — it pulls you toward "what can I compute?" instead of "what should change?" You'll get a cleaner frame without it.

**The one real caveat:** grilling will hit questions only the CSV can answer — is it one row per athlete per test date or one row per athlete; are positions in it; is there an ID that joins to your other systems; do you have subtest-level values or only composites. The skill's own rule is to look facts up rather than ask you, but there's no codebase to look in, so those become parked. Not blocking — they bound what the *prototype* can attempt, not what the frame should be.

**Cheap unblock when you get to a machine with it:** paste the header row and the row count. Not the file. That converts most of those parked facts into answers.

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled — the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Each question should be formatted like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree — settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. ## Round 1 — the root frontier

❓ **Q1** - **Which coaching decision should an S2 insight change?**: This is the anchor for everything else. Candidates: (a) *personnel / position fit* — who plays where; (b) *install & rep allocation* — how much scheme complexity a player can absorb; (c) *individualized coaching cues* — how you teach and deploy this specific player; (d) *recruiting & portal evaluation*; (e) *pre-snap responsibility assignment* — who carries the checks.

➡️ **(c), with (b) as the near neighbor.** Here's the reasoning: (a) and (d) are talent-identification claims, and the moment you frame S2 as "this predicts who's good," you own a predictive-validity argument you probably can't win with your sample — and coaches have seen that pitch fail before. (c) requires no predictive claim at all. "This player processes fast but reads narrow, so simplify his pre-snap menu" is actionable on Monday and is unfalsifiable in the way that matters — it's a coaching adjustment, not a prophecy.

❓ **Q2** - **Who actually receives the artifact?**: Position coaches, coordinators, S&C staff, sports science internal, or the athlete? Different audiences want opposite things — coordinators want aggregate and comparative, position coaches want individual and prescriptive.

➡️ **One position coach.** An insight only counts when someone changes a behavior, and position coaches are the layer that acts on individual players. Coordinators will ask for aggregate rollups that push you back toward percentiles. Pick the coach most likely to engage, not the most senior.

❓ **Q3** - **What is actually wrong with percentiles?**: "Beyond percentiles" can mean four different complaints: they're *normative* (compare to others, not to self); they're *static* (no change over time); they're *undifferentiated* (one composite hides the profile); or they're *inert* (no "so what" attached).

➡️ **Primarily undifferentiated, secondarily inert.** A 60th-percentile composite can hide a player at the 95th in reaction time and the 20th in perception span — and that player needs the opposite coaching from an evenly-60th player. The composite actively destroys the actionable signal. If you agree, then "beyond percentiles" concretely means *profile shape plus a prescription*, which is a much sharper build target than "insights."

❓ **Q4** - **One-off retrospective, or a recurring per-cycle product?**: Does this run once against the data you have, or does it become something that regenerates every testing cycle?

➡️ **One-off for v1.** Earn the recurring product by getting one coach to act on one insight. Building a pipeline before anyone has changed a decision is exactly the "data collection without a clear plan" failure your own EOY Kitman meeting logged. This also keeps you out of `/to-spec` → `/to-tickets` entirely for now.

❓ **Q5** - **Scope for v1 — which population?**: All athletes with S2 data, football only, or a single position group?

➡️ **A single position group.** Narrow produces a artifact concrete enough to argue with. Broad produces a summary nobody acts on. It also makes the sample-size problem visible early rather than after you've built something.

❓ **Q6** - **Do you have a buyer, or is this self-initiated?**: Did someone ask for this, or are you bringing it to them unprompted? This changes whether the deliverable needs to sell the idea before it delivers the insight.

➡️ **Tell me honestly which.** If self-initiated, v1's real job is to earn a second meeting, which argues for one vivid player example over a comprehensive report. If someone asked, I want to know what they actually said they wanted — that phrasing usually contains the real decision from Q1.

# CONTEXT

Glossary for the S2 Cognition evaluation. Terms only — no implementation
detail, no plan, no decisions record (those are ADRs).

## Beyond Percentiles

The project's animating complaint, resolved 2026-08-08.

Percentiles fail on two counts, in priority order:

1. **Undifferentiated** (primary) — a single composite percentile collapses a
   profile that is not flat. An athlete at the 60th percentile composite may sit
   at the 95th in one category and the 20th in another. Two athletes sharing a
   composite can require opposite handling.
2. **Inert** (secondary) — a percentile carries no prescription. It states rank
   and stops.

"Beyond percentiles" therefore means **profile shape plus a prescription**, not
"more numbers" and not "better-looking numbers."

## Profile Shape

The pattern of an athlete's category scores *relative to their own mean*, as
distinct from their rank against the normative population. Dispersion across
categories is the object of interest; the composite is the thing that hides it.

## Position Fit

**UNRESOLVED — pending.** The term currently spans two distinct questions that
must not be conflated:

- *Fit-within-position* — is this athlete's profile typical or atypical for the
  position he already plays?
- *Fit-to-position* — which position does this athlete's profile best suit?

These require different comparisons and different data. Do not use the bare term
"position fit" until this is resolved.

## Audience Tiers

Ordered, and not interchangeable:

1. **Sports science internal** — first and current audience. Consumes
   exploratory findings; decides whether the signal warrants going further.
2. **Position coaches / S&C staff** — second audience, not yet engaged.
3. **Athletes** — explicitly out of scope. Not a recipient of this work.

## Vendor Baseline

The static PDF reports S2 produces per athlete. These define the floor: an
output resembling the vendor PDF has added nothing. The baseline is a thing to
exceed, not merely a source of context.

---

## Open terms

- **Position Fit** — see above.
- **S2 score** — likely overloaded (category percentile vs composite percentile
  vs raw value). Resolve once the CSV schema is in hand.

content.text:
`CONTEXT.md` written with five resolved terms. Note that I logged **Position Fit as UNRESOLVED** — your Q1 answer uses a term that's doing two jobs, and round 2 exists mostly to split it.

---

## On the aside: CSV or PDFs?

**Both, but they do different jobs, and the CSV is the one you can't substitute.**

The CSV is the analysis substrate. Category-level percentiles are *exactly* what profile-shape work needs — you don't need raw scores for dispersion, because you're comparing an athlete to his own mean across categories, not to the normative population. Percentiles are sufficient for that.

The PDFs earn their keep two ways, and the second is the one people miss:

1. **Semantic layer** — what each category actually means, so you're not inventing interpretations. This partially substitutes for the parallel `/research` step.
2. **The baseline you have to beat.** The vendor PDF *is* the current state of the art in your building. If your output looks like their PDF, you've added nothing and the project has no reason to exist. That's why I wrote it into `CONTEXT.md` as Vendor Baseline — it's a floor to exceed, not background reading.

**Quantity:** all of the CSV, but only **2–3 PDFs**. Pick a high composite, a low composite, and one visibly uneven profile if you can spot one. You need the vendor's vocabulary and ceiling, not a corpus.

---

## Round 2

❓ **Q7** - **Fit-*within*-position or fit-*to*-position?**: The split I flagged in the glossary. *Within* asks "is this athlete's profile typical for the room he's already in?" *To* asks "which room should he be in?"

➡️ **Fit-within-position.** Your Q5 answer makes this nearly forced — a single position group in v1 structurally cannot answer fit-*to*, which needs multiple groups to compare across. Fit-*to* also inherits a cross-position comparability problem you don't need in v1. Confirm and I'll resolve the term in `CONTEXT.md`.

❓ **Q8** - **Which position group?**: Needs high cognitive load, *differentiated* demands within the room, and enough athletes to see a distribution.

➡️ **Safeties or linebackers** — highest pre-snap processing and communication load, so a cognitive profile plausibly matters. But one criterion may override the theory: pick the room whose coach sports science already has the best relationship with, because that coach is audience tier 2. A perfect finding delivered to a closed door is worth nothing.

❓ **Q9** - **What does internal sports science actually decide from v1, and what kills it?**: You're audience tier 1 and this is self-initiated, so the real output is a go/no-go on whether to keep going.

➡️ **Define the kill criterion now, before you look at data.** Something like: *if fewer than ~30% of athletes show meaningful dispersion between their highest and lowest category, the "composite hides the profile" premise is false and we stop.* Pre-committing to what would falsify the idea is the only thing separating this from fishing — and you'll be tempted to move the goalposts once you see the numbers. I'd write this as the first ADR.

❓ **Q10** - **Does v1 prescribe, or only surface shape?**: This one tests the glossary. Your Q3 answer defined "beyond percentiles" as *shape **plus** prescription*, and I wrote that into `CONTEXT.md`.

➡️ **Shape only for v1 — but recorded as a deliberate scope cut, not a redefinition of the term.** Prescription under a *position fit* frame means telling a coach to move a player, which is precisely the talent-ID claim you aren't equipped to defend yet. "Here are three athletes whose profile is atypical for their room, worth a conversation" is honest, still actionable, and doesn't overclaim. If you disagree, say so — but I don't want to quietly weaken the glossary definition to match a smaller v1.

---

**Deferred to round 3** (depends on Q7): what "typical" is benchmarked against — your own incumbents, S2's position norms, or on-field outcomes. That's the circularity trap in this project, and it deserves its own round rather than being smuggled in here.

=== ADR-FORMAT.md ===
# ADR Format

ADRs live in `docs/adr/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc.

Create the `docs/adr/` directory lazily — only when the first ADR is needed.

## Template

```md
# {Short title of the decision}

{1-3 sentences: what's the context, what did we decide, and why.}
```

That's it. An ADR can be a single paragraph. The value is in recording *that* a decision was made and *why* — not in filling out sections.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most ADRs won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN`) — useful when decisions are revisited
- **Considered Options** — only when the rejected alternatives are worth remembering
- **Consequences** — only when non-obvious downstream effects need to be called out

## Numbering

Scan `docs/adr/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to offer an ADR

All three of these must be true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will look at the code and wonder "why on earth did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it — you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

### What qualifies

- **Architectural shape.** "We're using a monorepo." "The write model is event-sourced, the read model is projected into Postgres."
- **Integration patterns between contexts.** "Ordering and Billing communicate via domain events, not synchronous HTTP."
- **Technology choices that carry lock-in.** Database, message bus, auth provider, deployment target. Not every library — just the ones that would take a quarter to swap out.
- **Boundary and scope decisions.** "Customer data is owned by the Customer context; other contexts reference it by ID only." The explicit no-s are as valuable as the yes-s.
- **Deliberate deviations from the obvious path.** "We're using manual SQL instead of an ORM because X." Anything where a reasonable reader would assume the opposite. These stop the next engineer from "fixing" something that was deliberate.
- **Constraints not visible in the code.** "We can't use AWS because of compliance requirements." "Response times must be under 200ms because of the partner API contract."
- **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it — otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.

=== CONTEXT-FORMAT.md ===
# CONTEXT.md Format

## Structure

```md
# {Context Name}

{One or two sentence description of what this context is and why it exists.}

## Language

**Order**:
{A one or two sentence description of the term}
_Avoid_: Purchase, transaction

**Invoice**:
A request for payment sent to a customer after delivery.
_Avoid_: Bill, payment request

**Customer**:
A person or organization that places orders.
_Avoid_: Client, buyer, account
```

## Rules

- **Be opinionated.** When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under `_Avoid_`.
- **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences max. Define what it IS, not what it does.
- **Only include terms specific to this project's context.** General programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) don't belong even if the project uses them extensively. Before adding a term, ask: is this a concept unique to this context, or a general programming concept? Only the former belongs.
- **Group terms under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge. If all terms belong to a single cohesive area, a flat list is fine.

## Single vs multi-context repos

**Single context (most repos):** One `CONTEXT.md` at the repo root.

**Multiple contexts:** A `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the repo root lists the contexts, where they live, and how they relate to each other:

```md
# Context Map

## Contexts

- [Ordering](./src/ordering/CONTEXT.md) — receives and tracks customer orders
- [Billing](./src/billing/CONTEXT.md) — generates invoices and processes payments
- [Fulfillment](./src/fulfillment/CONTEXT.md) — manages warehouse picking and shipping

## Relationships

- **Ordering → Fulfillment**: Ordering emits `OrderPlaced` events; Fulfillment consumes them to start picking
- **Fulfillment → Billing**: Fulfillment emits `ShipmentDispatched` events; Billing consumes them to generate invoices
- **Ordering ↔ Billing**: Shared types for `CustomerId` and `Money`
```

The skill infers which structure applies:

- If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, read it to find contexts
- If only a root `CONTEXT.md` exists, single context
- If neither exists, create a root `CONTEXT.md` lazily when the first term is resolved

When multiple contexts exist, infer which one the current topic relates to. If unclear, ask.

That's it. An ADR can be a single paragraph. The value is in recording *that* a decision was made and *why* — not in filling out sections.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most ADRs won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN`) — useful when decisions are revisited
- **Considered Options** — only when the rejected alternatives are worth remembering
- **Consequences** — only when non-obvious downstream effects need to be called out

## Numbering

Scan `docs/adr/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to offer an ADR

All three of these must be true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will look at the code and wonder "why on earth did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it — you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

### What qualifies

- **Architectural shape.** "We're using a monorepo." "The write model is event-sourced, the read model is projected into Postgres."
- **Integration patterns between contexts.** "Ordering and Billing communicate via domain events, not synchronous HTTP."
- **Technology choices that carry lock-in.** Database, message bus, auth provider, deployment target. Not every library — just the ones that would take a quarter to swap out.
- **Boundary and scope decisions.** "Customer data is owned by the Customer context; other contexts reference it by ID only." The explicit no-s are as valuable as the yes-s.
- **Deliberate deviations from the obvious path.** "We're using manual SQL instead of an ORM because X." Anything where a reasonable reader would assume the opposite. These stop the next engineer from "fixing" something that was deliberate.
- **Constraints not visible in the code.** "We can't use AWS because of compliance requirements." "Response times must be under 200ms because of the partner API contract."
- **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it — otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.

=== CONTEXT-FORMAT.md ===
# CONTEXT.md Format

## Structure

```md
# {Context Name}

{One or two sentence description of what this context is and why it exists.}

## Language

**Order**:
{A one or two sentence description of the term}
_Avoid_: Purchase, transaction

**Invoice**:
A request for payment sent to a customer after delivery.
_Avoid_: Bill, payment request

**Customer**:
A person or organization that places orders.
_Avoid_: Client, buyer, account
```

## Rules

- **Be opinionated.** When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under `_Avoid_`.
- **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences max. Define what it IS, not what it does.
- **Only include terms specific to this project's context.** General programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) don't belong even if the project uses them extensively. Before adding a term, ask: is this a concept unique to this context, or a general programming concept? Only the former belongs.
- **Group terms under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge. If all terms belong to a single cohesive area, a flat list is fine.

## Single vs multi-context repos

**Single context (most repos):** One `CONTEXT.md` at the repo root.

**Multiple contexts:** A `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the repo root lists the contexts, where they live, and how they relate to each other:

```md
# Context Map

## Contexts

- [Ordering](./src/ordering/CONTEXT.md) — receives and tracks customer orders
- [Billing](./src/billing/CONTEXT.md) — generates invoices and processes payments
- [Fulfillment](./src/fulfillment/CONTEXT.md) — manages warehouse picking and shipping

## Relationships

- **Ordering → Fulfillment**: Ordering emits `OrderPlaced` events; Fulfillment consumes them to start picking
- **Fulfillment → Billing**: Fulfillment emits `ShipmentDispatched` events; Billing consumes them to generate invoices
- **Ordering ↔ Billing**: Shared types for `CustomerId` and `Money`
```

The skill infers which structure applies:

- If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, read it to find contexts
- If only a root `CONTEXT.md` exists, single context
- If neither exists, create a root `CONTEXT.md` lazily when the first term is resolved

When multiple contexts exist, infer which one the current topic relates to. If unclear, ask.

measure directly on percentile values systematically understates it in the

Four ADRs now. Writing 0004 surfaced a useful consequence I've folded in: because z-space fixes the population SD at 1, you never have to estimate the room's own standard deviation from ~15 linemen — which would have been the noisiest number in the analysis.

---

## Round 4

❓ **Q15** - **Who counts as "in the room"?**: All OL with S2 data, or only scholarship players, or only realistic contributors? This directly sets what "typical" means.

➡️ **Everyone with data. Flag roster status, don't filter on it.** Filtering to "guys who actually play" reintroduces exactly the selection circularity we've been avoiding — you'd be defining the typical lineman as *whoever the staff already chose*, then discovering that the guys they chose are typical. Record scholarship status and class year as attributes so you can check afterward whether deviation tracks them. That check is itself an interesting finding; the filter would have destroyed it.

❓ **Q16** - **If an athlete tested more than once, which result counts?**: Latest, first, or an average?

➡️ **Most recent, pre-committed now.** Current state is what a coach acts on, and fixing the rule before you see the data stops you from quietly picking whichever date makes the story cleaner. Change-over-time is a genuinely interesting question but it's the *static* complaint you explicitly deprioritized in Q3 — it's a different project, and mixing it in would double the scope of v1.

❓ **Q17** - **How is Room Deviation actually computed?**: A single distance from the room centroid (one interpretable number, but it hides which category drove it), or per-category deviations (richer, harder to rank athletes by)?

➡️ **Per-category deviation in population-SD units, with max-absolute-deviation as the headline for ranking.** You get both: a sortable single number and an immediate answer to "deviant *how*?" — which is the whole point of going beyond a composite. Explicitly **not** Mahalanobis distance: with ~15 linemen and multiple categories, the covariance matrix is too poorly estimated to be trustworthy, and it would manufacture false precision while making the result unexplainable to a position coach.

❓ **Q18** - **Does the artifact lead with the room or with individuals?**: "Here is the shape of the OL room" versus "here are the three most deviant linemen."

➡️ **Room distribution first, individuals second.** Your tier-1 audience is sports science, and their job is to judge whether the method holds before trusting any name it produces. Leading with named athletes invites them to argue about whether those three players *seem* right — which is an argument about their priors, not about your analysis.

---

**Deferred to round 5** (depends on Q17): the minimum room size you'll accept and what you fall back to if the OL room is too thin. That threshold depends on which method you pick here, so it waits.

❓ **Q19** - **Minimum room size, and the fallback if OL is too thin.**: The deferred question. An absolute threshold can legitimately return zero flagged athletes, and that is a real result.

❓ **Q22** - **How does the artifact get delivered?**: A file in the repo, or a shareable link?

➡️ **Both — build the HTML in the project folder, then publish it as an Artifact for a private link.** Your tier-1 audience needs to open it without cloning anything, and the link is what makes it forwardable when you're ready for tier 2. ## Round 6 — closing

❓ **Q23** - **What sections does the write-up have, and what does it explicitly refuse to claim?**: Structure matters more than usual here because the pre-registration is the credibility of the whole thing.

➡️ **State the question and all pre-registered thresholds *before* any result** — gate, flagging threshold, room floor. A reader who sees the criteria only after the numbers has no way to know they weren't fitted. Then: gate result, room shape, flagged individuals (or an explicit "none"), and a closing **"what this does not claim"** section. That last section says plainly that deviation from the room is not evidence of being worse, that no predictive claim about on-field performance is being made, and that the room mean describes *your current roster*, not an ideal. Without it, the first reader to skim will convert "atypical" into "bad" and you'll spend the second meeting walking it back.

❓ **Q24** - **If the gate fails, do you still write it up?**: I already put "a short written negative finding is a legitimate end state" into ADR 0001's consequences, but you haven't actually confirmed it, and I don't want it standing as my assumption.

➡️ **Yes — same structure, shorter, published to the same audience.** A pre-registration you only honor when the answer is interesting isn't a pre-registration. And "we tested whether the composite hides anything and it doesn't" is genuinely useful internally: it closes a question that would otherwise keep resurfacing.

❓ **Q25** - **Who specifically is "sports science internal"?**: The audience tier is currently an abstraction, and the go/no-go isn't real until a person owns it.

➡️ **Name one reviewer now.** One named person who will read v1 and say continue or stop.   <priority_instructions>
    Every byte a tool returns enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. The context-mode tools let you do the work in a sandbox and surface only the derived answer — the raw bytes stay out. Think-in-Code: program the analysis, do not compute it by reading raw data into your conversation.

    1. GATHER: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute(commands, queries)
       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.

    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)
       - Derive answers FROM data: filter, count, aggregate, parse, transform. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation; the raw bytes stay in the sandbox.

Bash stays correct when you intend to OBSERVE a short fixed output (git status on a clean tree, whoami, pwd) or when you are mutating state (git, mkdir, rm, mv, navigation).

content.text:
99 PDFs across 12 position rooms — and the filenames encode athlete and test date, which means I can answer ADR 0007's gating question without opening a single report.

This is cohort metadata, not results, so it's safe to compute before the kill criterion is set.

input.command:
cd /Users/kristinarash/DEV/COG_S2_Position_Reports
python3 - <<'PY'
import re, pathlib
from collections import defaultdict

root = pathlib.Path('.')
rooms = defaultdict(list)
for p in root.rglob('*.pdf'):
    room = p.parent.name.replace('S2 Baylor ', '')
    stem = p.stem
    if stem.startswith('S2Cog_'): stem = stem[6:]
    m = re.search(r'(\d{8})$', stem)                      # Last_First_YYYYMMDD
    if m:
        date, who = m.group(1), stem[:m.start()].rstrip('_')
    else:                                                  # odd export format
        m2 = re.search(r'(\d{2})_(\d{2})_(\d{4})', stem)
        date = f"{m2.group(3)}{m2.group(1)}{m2.group(2)}" if m2 else "UNKNOWN"
        who = re.split(r'\s*Report Generation', stem)[0].replace(',', '').replace(' ', '_')
    rooms[room].append((who.lower().strip('_'), date))

print(f"{'ROOM':<12} {'files':>5} {'athletes':>9} {'repeat':>7}   clears n>=10?")
print("-"*58)
tot_a = 0
for room in sorted(rooms, key=lambda r: -len({w for w,_ in rooms[r]})):
    rec = rooms[room]
    ath = {w for w, _ in rec}
    repeat = len(rec) - len(ath)
    tot_a += len(ath)
    flag = "YES" if len(ath) >= 10 else "no"
    print(f"{room:<12} {len(rec):>5} {len(ath):>9} {repeat:>7}   {flag}")
print("-"*58)
print(f"{'TOTAL':<12} {sum(len(v) for v in rooms.values()):>5} {tot_a:>9}")

ol = rooms.get('OL', [])
print(f"\nOL detail — {len(ol)} files, {len({w for w,_ in ol})} unique athletes")
seen = defaultdict(list)
for w, d in ol: seen[w].append(d)
for w in sorted(seen):
    ds = sorted(seen[w])
    print(f"   {w:<24} {'  '.join(ds)}{'   <-- repeat, use most recent' if len(ds)>1 else ''}")
PY

Three findings, and one of them is a problem the grilling couldn't have caught without data.

**OL clears the floor comfortably — 16 athletes.** No fallback needed. Worth noting the round-3 revision was decisive: safeties have only **8**, so they'd have failed n≥10 outright. Switching to OL on room-size grounds was the right call for exactly the reason predicted.

**Zero repeat athletes** — every player tested once, so ADR 0005's "most recent test" rule stands but never fires.

**But the OL room was not tested contemporaneously.** Eleven tested 2026-07-08; the rest span 2022, 2024, and 2025. That's a temporal confound the design never addressed.

Schema learned, and it surfaced something that could invalidate the whole design — so I need to check it before anything else.

**The report is 9 skill categories plus an S2 composite, on a percentile scale** (0–100), with the vendor's own five bands. Plus two secondary measures (speed/accuracy tradeoff).

If OL reports are instead normed *within* position, then every OL room percentile is already centered near 50 and Room Deviation would be measuring something largely pre-removed. That's a design-breaking difference, and it's metadata I can check without touching any scores.

**The design survives — and that check was worth doing.** All 16 OL reports use an identical reference group (`FOOTBALL OL [NFL PROSPECTS - ALL POSITIONS]`), and the `[NFL PROSPECTS - ALL POSITIONS]` bracket is constant across every position. Two side findings: report templates don't always match folders (a WR-template report in CB, two OL-templates in P/K), though **OL is clean — all 16 have OL templates**. And there are 9 skill categories plus the S2 composite, not an unknown number.

Before I set ADR 0001's threshold, one null-model fact I need to get right — this is computation on random numbers, not on your athletes.

content.text:
I have not looked at a single OL score yet — only a QB report for schema and the reference-group line from each file. That matters, because the null model just invalidated ADR 0001's intended criterion.

## The kill criterion as conceived doesn't work

The plan was "if fewer than ~30% of athletes show meaningful dispersion, the premise is false." With 9 categories, **89% of purely random athletes clear a 2.0 SD range.** Spread is the *null expectation*, not evidence. That gate would have passed even if S2's categories measured nothing but noise — it would have rubber-stamped the project rather than testing it.

The informative question isn't whether profiles are uneven. It's whether they're uneven *relative to what independence would produce*:

| Scenario | Mean range across 9 categories |
|---|---|
| Categories independent — composite hides a lot | **2.97 SD** |
| Categories moderately redundant (r≈0.5) | 2.10 SD |
| One dominant factor (r≈0.8) — composite says it all | 1.33 SD |

**Proposed replacement:** gate on the **mean category range across the 16 OL athletes**, proceeding only if it is **≥ 2.5 SD** — roughly the point where average inter-category redundancy exceeds ~30%. Below that, the composite substantially captures the profile and the project's premise is false.

This uses a mean of 16 numbers rather than a 9×9 correlation matrix, so it stays consistent with ADR 0006's reasoning about small-n covariance. It tests whether the composite hides variation — **not** whether that variation is valid, which remains the `/research` question.

This changes the criterion's *form*, not just its number, so it needs ADR 0010 rather than a quiet edit to 0001.

## Two decisions before I compute anything

**D1 — Temporal cohort.** Eleven OL tested 2026-07-08; the others in 2022, 2024, 2025. Options: all 16, or 2026-only (n=11, still clears the floor).

➡️ **All 16, with test year flagged and checked as a diagnostic.** ADR 0005 already settled the principle — flag, don't filter — for roster status, and the same logic applies here; dropping five players costs 30% of the room. But four years is real development time for a 19-year-old, so if deviation turns out to track test year, we revisit rather than explain it away.

**D2 — Adopt the revised kill criterion at mean range ≥ 2.5 SD?** Or a different threshold — 2.97 (full independence) would be strict, 2.10 lenient.

Confirm both and I'll write ADR 0010, commit it, and only then extract the OL scores. Committing first is the whole point of the exercise.

from pypdf import PdfReader
import pathlib, re
from collections import Counter

flagged=[]; tot=Counter()
for p in sorted(pathlib.Path('.').rglob('*.pdf')):
    room = p.parent.name.replace('S2 Baylor ','')
    r = PdfReader(str(p))
    p1 = r.pages[0].extract_text() or ""
    p2 = r.pages[1].extract_text() or ""
    seg = re.search(r'S2 SCORE(.*?)0%\s*-\s*20%', p2, re.S)
    body = seg.group(1) if seg else ""
    na = len(re.findall(r'N/A', body)); nvals = len(re.findall(r'\d+\s*%', body))
    invalid = 'did not pass data validity' in p1 or p1.rstrip().endswith('INVALID')
    tot[room]+=1
    if invalid or na:
        m = re.search(r'(\d+) task\(s\) did not pass', p1)
        flagged.append((room, p.stem[6:], "INVALID" if invalid else "partial",
                        m.group(1) if m else "?", na, nvals))

print(f"{'ROOM':<10} {'ATHLETE':<26} {'FLAG':<8} {'tasks':>5} {'N/A':>4} {'vals':>5}")
print("-"*62)
for f in flagged: print(f"{f[0]:<10} {f[1]:<26} {f[2]:<8} {f[3]:>5} {f[4]:>4} {f[5]:>5}")
print("-"*62)

print("OL affected:", [f[1] for f in flagged if f[0]=='OL'] or "none")

content.text:
Only **1 of 99** reports failed validity — and it landed in the OL room. Six tasks failed, leaving 3 of 9 categories, so a 9-category range simply cannot be computed for him.

Excluding him is forced rather than chosen, but it's still a cohort change, so it gets recorded. Note this is *not* the same as ADR 0005's flag-don't-filter rule: that guards against filtering on **selection** attributes, which would be circular. Vendor-flagged invalidity is an external data-quality fact and carries no selection bias.

Stop — **10 of 15 flagged is not a finding, it's a broken threshold**, and it fails for exactly the same reason ADR 0001 did: taking a *maximum* over 9 categories inflates the statistic, and 1.5 SD never accounted for that.

I will not quietly retune it. Let me first prove the claim by calibrating against a homogeneous-room null.

import csv, numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
rows=list(csv.DictReader(open('data/ol_scores.csv')))
CATS=["perception_speed","search_efficiency","tracking_capacity","visual_learning",
      "instinctive_learning","decision_complexity","impulse_control",
      "distraction_control","improvisation"]
Z=norm.ppf(np.array([[float(r[c]) for c in CATS] for r in rows])/100.0)
n,K=Z.shape; D=Z-Z.mean(0); mx=np.abs(D).max(1)

sd_room = Z.std(0,ddof=1)
print(f"within-room SD per category (population SD = 1 by construction):")
print(f"  mean {sd_room.mean():.2f}   range {sd_room.min():.2f}-{sd_room.max():.2f}")
print("  -> the room is about as spread as the general population; position")
print("     selection has NOT compressed these traits.\n")

# NULL: homogeneous room, same n, K and spread. How often does 1.5 SD flag?
g=np.random.default_rng(11); S=20000
sim=g.standard_normal((S,n,K))*sd_room
simD=sim-sim.mean(1,keepdims=True)
rate=(np.abs(simD).max(2)>=1.5).mean(1)
print(f"NULL CALIBRATION — homogeneous room, no atypical athlete exists")
print(f"  expected share flagged at 1.5 SD : {rate.mean()*100:.0f}%")
print(f"  central 90% of null flag counts  : {np.percentile(rate*n,5):.0f}-{np.percentile(rate*n,95):.0f} of {n}")
print(f"  OBSERVED                          : {int((mx>=1.5).sum())} of {n}")
print(f"  -> observed is {'INSIDE' if np.percentile(rate*n,5)<=(mx>=1.5).sum()<=np.percentile(rate*n,95) else 'OUTSIDE'} the null range."
      f" The 1.5 threshold has essentially no discriminating power.\n")

# what threshold WOULD hold a ~5% false-flag rate per athlete?
for t in (1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0):
    print(f"  null flag rate at {t:.1f} SD: {(np.abs(simD).max(2)>=t).mean()*100:5.1f}%   observed: {int((mx>=t).sum())}/{n}")

# room shape: is any category mean different from the NFL-prospect norm?
se=sd_room/np.sqrt(n); t=Z.mean(0)/se
p=2*(1-norm.cdf(np.abs(t)))
SHORT=["percep","search","track","vis_lrn","inst_lrn","dec_cplx","impulse","distract","improv"]
print("\nROOM SHAPE vs norm — 9 comparisons, Bonferroni alpha = 0.0056")
for s,m,tt,pp in sorted(zip(SHORT,Z.mean(0),t,p),key=lambda x:x[3]):
    print(f"  {s:<9} z={m:+.2f}  t={tt:+.2f}  p={pp:.3f} {'*survives' if pp<0.0056 else ''}")

content.text:
The null calibration is decisive, and it changes the finding.

**The 1.5 SD threshold has no discriminating power.** A perfectly homogeneous room — one containing no atypical athlete at all — would flag 7 to 13 of 15 at that threshold. We observed 10. Squarely inside the null.

And at every stricter threshold the room looks *less* extreme than chance:

| Threshold | Homogeneous room would flag | OL room actually flagged |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 SD | 69% (~10) | 10 of 15 |
| 2.0 SD | 33% (~5) | **2 of 15** |
| 2.5 SD | 11% (~2) | **0 of 15** |
| 3.0 SD | 3% | **0 of 15** |

**There are no atypical linemen.** Not "we didn't find any" — the room has fewer extreme profiles than random variation alone would produce. ADR 0008 anticipated precisely this outcome and pre-committed to reporting it as a real result.

# The 1.5 SD flagging threshold was uncalibrated; the Room Deviation finding is null

ADR 0008 fixed the flag at 1.5 population SD from the room mean on any single
category. Applied literally to the fifteen linemen, it flags ten.

Ten of fifteen is not a finding. The threshold repeats the error ADR 0010 caught
in the original kill criterion: it takes a **maximum across nine categories**
without accounting for the inflation that maximum introduces.

Simulating a homogeneous room — same n, same nine categories, same observed
within-room spread, containing no atypical athlete by construction — a 1.5 SD
rule flags **69%** of athletes, with a central 90% interval of 7 to 13 of 15.
The observed 10 sits squarely inside that interval and carries no information.

At stricter thresholds the room is *less* extreme than chance:

| Threshold | Null flag rate | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 SD | 69% | 10 / 15 |
| 2.0 SD | 33% | 2 / 15 |
| 2.5 SD | 11% | 0 / 15 |
| 3.0 SD | 3% | 0 / 15 |

**The finding is null.** No offensive lineman deviates from the room beyond what
normal variation produces. This is reported as the result, exactly as ADR 0008's
consequences pre-committed: "An absolute threshold can return zero flagged
athletes. That is a real result."

## What is NOT being done

The threshold is not being retuned to produce a more interesting answer. The
pre-registered rule was applied, its output is reported, and its calibration is
reported alongside. Any future flagging rule must be calibrated against a
homogeneous-room null *before* use — a threshold chosen on intuition is
worthless when the statistic is a maximum over many categories.

## Consequences

The room's within-category spread is about as wide as the general population
(mean SD 0.98), so position selection has not compressed these traits. What is
absent is any individual standing outside that spread.

The surviving result is at room level, not individual level, and it is weak:
of nine categories, only visual learning approaches a difference from the
NFL-prospect norm (z=-0.40, p=0.009), and that does not survive Bonferroni
correction across nine comparisons (alpha 0.0056). The room composite sits at
the 44th percentile.

Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.226/581ebba2660139c1f45ac31b044007b0/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values — touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe — run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure — do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job — magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). → `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) — each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. → `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette — run the script, don't reason about ΔE.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,…>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory — or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, ≥8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. → `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer — by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. → `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For ≥ 2 series a legend is always present and ≤ 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box — the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** — its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout — open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** — it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue — it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale → two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake — see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light→dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD ΔE ≥ 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6–8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL — full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead — see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view — it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for ≥ 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** — values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance — every value filled in — is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical — steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of — build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong — check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** — every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |
