content.content: Launching skill: artifact-design

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

The skill's own calibration says this is a **utilitarian** treatment — an internal findings memo, not an editorial page — which matches what I built. Checking against the fundamentals found two real gaps: only one type role (it asks for 2+), and no `prefers-reduced-motion` guard on the tooltip transition.

content.text:
Verified: repo clean across 5 commits, no athlete data tracked in git, registry shipped, report renders in both themes.

**The report:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/30d83487-f660-42d7-9810-408f8b622524

## The finding

**The gate passed. The finding is null.**

The composite *does* hide real variation — the nine categories are only weakly related (r ≈ 0.18), so a single S2 number genuinely discards profile information. Your original complaint was correct.

But **no lineman is cognitively atypical.** And this is where the pre-registration earned its keep. The 1.5 SD flag fired on 10 of 15 — which looks like a finding until you calibrate it. A room containing *no* atypical athlete at all would flag 7–13, because the statistic is a maximum across nine categories. At 2.5 SD, chance predicts 1–2 flagged and the room produced **zero**.

Had I reported those ten names, you'd have taken a list of "atypical" linemen to a position coach built on nothing.

**I did not retune the threshold.** It was applied as written, its output reported, and its miscalibration recorded in ADR 0013 alongside the rule that any future threshold must be null-calibrated before use.

## What that cost, and what it bought

Two thresholds in this project turned out to be uncalibrated in the same way — the original kill criterion (caught before data, ADR 0010) and the flagging threshold (caught after, ADR 0013). Both failed because taking a max or range over nine categories inflates the statistic. That's the transferable lesson, and it's now written down.

The room itself sits at the 44th percentile composite, within half an SD of the NFL-prospect norm on all nine categories. Visual learning is lowest (p = 0.009) but doesn't survive correction for nine comparisons, so the page labels it descriptive.

Two things surfaced that you'll want regardless: **one lineman's report failed S2's own validity checks** (6 of 10 tasks) and should be retested — he's excluded, not dismissed. And report templates don't always match folders elsewhere in the export, though OL was clean.

The page is fully de-identified. The null result meant no individual callouts were warranted, so nothing was lost by removing names — and a shareable link carrying athletes' cognitive scores was worth avoiding.

**Still open:** the commit author on your pre-registration still reads "Kristina Rash." Give me the right name and I'll amend it.

Want me to run `/harvest` on this to distill it into your SecondBrain? The threshold-calibration lesson looks like the durable part.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/Harvest

# Harvest

Turn a **finished** project into (1) an entry in the shipped-work ledger and
(2) zero or more evergreen lesson articles in `Knowledge/`.

**Vault:** `/Users/kristinarash/Desktop/SecondBrain/` (conventions: vault `CLAUDE.md`)
**Ledger:** `output/_ledger.md`
**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `/Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/_shared/config.json` — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.

Core rule: lesson articles are written ONLY from shipped work. If the project
hasn't shipped, stop — offer to note it in `Projects/` instead.

## Process

### 1. Confirm the ship

Establish: what shipped, when, and the evidence (deliverable handed off, talk
given, pipeline live, commit/PR, decision locked). If Eric declared it shipped,
that's sufficient — record his framing. If ambiguous ("mostly done"), ask one
question; a harvest of unfinished work poisons the ledger.

### 2. Gather the project's story

Pull from whichever exist, cheapest first:

- The project folder (DEV repo, vault `Projects/` folder) — plans, READMEs, retro notes
- `memsearch search "<project> lessons decisions" --top-k 5` — session history
- The current conversation, if the project just finished here

You're looking for: what was tried and abandoned, what surprised, what the
final approach was and *why*, what broke and how it was diagnosed.

### 3. Append the ledger entry (always)

Add a row to `output/_ledger.md`, newest first:
`| YYYY-MM-DD | artifact | one-line description | [[harvest-article-slug]] or empty |`

This step always happens. Steps 4–5 only happen if lessons clear the bar.

### 4. Distill lessons (0–3 articles, only when earned)

The bar: **a lesson qualifies only if it would change how a future, unrelated
project is done.** "We built X with Y" is ledger material, not a lesson.
"Schedulers fail silently unless the task itself writes a heartbeat" is a lesson.
Zero qualifying lessons is a legitimate outcome — say so and stop after the ledger.

Each article: one idea, kebab-case filename, into `Knowledge/` (subfolder by
kind if one fits, e.g. `Knowledge/frameworks/`):

```markdown
---
type: harvest
created: YYYY-MM-DD
source: <project name + repo/folder path>
shipped: YYYY-MM-DD
domain: [one, two]
tags: [three, four]
status: evergreen
---

# <The lesson as a claim, not a topic>

> **Harvested from:** <project> (shipped <date>)
> **In one sentence:** <the lesson>

<3–10 sentences: the context that produced it, why the obvious approach
failed or the chosen one worked, and where else this applies. Write it so
it makes sense to someone who never saw the project.>
```

### 5. Cross-link

- Wikilink first mentions of concepts/people/projects that have existing notes
  (scan filenames across `Notes/`, `Knowledge/`, `Projects/`).
- Add a `## Related` section (2–5 genuinely related links).
- Backfill the ledger row's harvest column with `[[article-slug]]`.

### 6. Close out

- If the project has a vault `Projects/` file, mark its status shipped/harvested.
- Commit the vault changes (ledger + articles) with message `harvest: <project>`.
- Report in one short paragraph: ledger entry, articles written (or "no lessons
  cleared the bar"), links added.

## Rules

- **Never overwrite** an existing note; slug collision → `-2` or ask to merge.
- Never harvest unfinished work. Never write a lesson article outside a harvest
  (that's the vault's harvest rule, see vault `CLAUDE.md`).
- Lessons are what was *learned*; the ledger records what was *done*. Don't mix.
- Prefer 1 sharp article over 3 mushy ones. Zero is fine.
Running the harvest. First confirming the ship and reading the vault conventions.

  <priority_instructions>
    Every byte a tool returns enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. The context-mode tools let you do the work in a sandbox and surface only the derived answer — the raw bytes stay out. Think-in-Code: program the analysis, do not compute it by reading raw data into your conversation.
  </priority_instructions>

  <tool_selection_hierarchy>
    0. MEMORY: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(sort: "timeline")
       - On resume or compaction, query prior decisions, errors, plans, user prompts before asking the user — auto-captured session memory is searchable.
    1. GATHER: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute(commands, queries)
       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.
       - Each command: {label: "section header", command: "shell command"}; the label becomes the FTS5 chunk title — descriptive labels improve search.
    2. FOLLOW-UP: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(queries: ["q1", "q2", ...])
       - Multiple related questions about anything already indexed (your captures + session memory). Batch every question in one array; the ranking pipeline runs per-query and the round-trip cost is paid once.
    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)
       - Derive answers FROM data: filter, count, aggregate, parse, transform. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation; the raw bytes stay in the sandbox.
  </tool_selection_hierarchy>

  <when_not_to_use>
    - You intend to PROCESS the output (filter, count, parse, aggregate) → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute or mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute. Bash stays correct when you intend to OBSERVE a short fixed output (git status on a clean tree, whoami, pwd) or when you are mutating state (git, mkdir, rm, mv, navigation).
    - You want to analyze, summarize, or extract from a file → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file. Read stays correct when you intend to Edit the file (Edit needs the exact bytes in your conversation to match against).
    - WebFetch → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index; full network access, results indexed for mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search, raw page bytes never enter your conversation.

    </artifact_policy>
  </output_constraints>

    Skills, roles, and decisions captured earlier in this session are a memory aid, not a standing order. Treat them as context that may help — the user's most recent message always takes precedence. If a captured directive conflicts with what the user now asks, follow the user; a past phrase does not bind you.

from pypdf import PdfReader
import pathlib, re, numpy as np, csv
from scipy.stats import norm
from collections import defaultdict

SRC=pathlib.Path('/Users/kristinarash/DEV/COG_S2_Position_Reports')
CATS=["percep","search","track","vis_lrn","inst_lrn","dec_cplx","impulse","distract","improv"]
rows=[]; invalid=[]; seen=defaultdict(list)
for p in sorted(SRC.rglob('*.pdf')):
    room=p.parent.name.replace('S2 Baylor ',''); r=PdfReader(str(p))
    if 'did not pass data validity' in (r.pages[0].extract_text() or ''):
        invalid.append((room,p.stem)); continue
    t=r.pages[1].extract_text() or ""
    seg=re.search(r'S2 SCORE(.*?)0%\s*-\s*20%',t,re.S)
    vals=[int(v) for v in re.findall(r'(\d+)\s*%',seg.group(1))] if seg else []
    if len(vals)!=10: invalid.append((room,p.stem+" [parse]")); continue
    stem=p.stem[6:]; m=re.search(r'(\d{8})$',stem)
    who=(stem[:m.start()].rstrip('_') if m else stem).lower()
    yr=int(m.group(1)[:4]) if m else 0
    seen[who].append(yr)
    rows.append((room,who,yr,vals))

print(f"parsed {len(rows)} of 99   excluded: {[i[1][:28] for i in invalid]}")
reps={k:v for k,v in seen.items() if len(v)>1}
print(f"athletes with MORE THAN ONE test (needed for reliability): {len(reps)}  -> {reps if reps else 'NONE'}\n")

Z=np.array([norm.ppf(np.array(r[3][:9])/100.0) for r in rows])
comp=np.array([r[3][9] for r in rows],float); rooms=np.array([r[0] for r in rows])

print("IS THE NORM COMMON ACROSS POSITIONS?  (if position-normed, every room sits at ~50th)")
print("-"*70); print(f"  {'room':<11}{'n':>3}{'mean composite pct':>21}{'mean z of 9 cats':>19}")
order=sorted(set(rooms), key=lambda r:-comp[rooms==r].mean())
for rm in order:
    k=rooms==rm
    print(f"  {rm:<11}{k.sum():>3}{comp[k].mean():>18.0f}th{Z[k].mean():>19.2f}")
print("-"*70)
print(f"  spread of room composite means: {comp[[True]*len(comp)].min():.0f}th-{comp.max():.0f}th individual; "
      f"room means range {min(comp[rooms==r].mean() for r in set(rooms)):.0f}th to {max(comp[rooms==r].mean() for r in set(rooms)):.0f}th")
grand=comp.mean()
print(f"  team mean composite percentile: {grand:.0f}th   (50th would imply position-specific norming)")

# between-room variance test on composite z
from scipy.stats import f_oneway
groups=[norm.ppf(comp[rooms==r]/100) for r in set(rooms) if (rooms==r).sum()>=4]
F,p=f_oneway(*groups)
print(f"  between-room difference in composite: F={F:.2f}, p={p:.3f} -> "
      f"{'rooms DIFFER; norm is common, pooling valid' if p<0.05 else 'no detectable room difference'}")

with open('data/team_scores.csv','w',newline='') as f:
    w=csv.writer(f); w.writerow(['room','athlete','year']+CATS+['composite'])
    for rm,who,yr,v in rows: w.writerow([rm,who,yr]+v)

content.text:
Both answerable now, and the second one has a hard blocker you'll want to know about immediately.

## Q1 — Scaling: yes, but not the way v1 was built

**Room-by-room does not scale.** Only 3 of 12 rooms clear the n≥10 floor — OL (15), WR (13), ILB (10). The other nine are 5–9 players, too small to define a room mean. And running 12 rooms × 9 categories is 108 comparisons, which is the same multiple-comparison trap that already bit this project twice, just larger.

**Pooling does scale, and I just verified it's legitimate.** If S2 normed percentiles *within* position, every room would sit near the 50th and cross-position comparison would be meaningless. They don't:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| P/K 82nd · QB 80th · SAF 79th | STARS 70th · CB 68th | WR 63rd · TE 58th · DL 57th · ILB 55th · RB 54th | DE 45th · **OL 42nd** |

Rooms range 42nd to 82nd against a team mean of 59th (F = 1.96, p = 0.048). The norm is common, so all 95 athletes sit on one scale. That means you can estimate position offsets and residual spread from **n = 95** rather than from 8 players — far more stable, and it makes the small rooms usable instead of excluded.

**One caveat worth stating before anyone gets excited about that gradient:** it runs skill-positions-high, big-men-low. That is very likely a property of measuring visual and decision speed against an all-positions norm, not a discovery about Baylor. Distinguishing "our OL are low" from "OL are low everywhere" requires S2's positional norms, which you don't have.

## Q2 — Individual analysis: possible, but blocked on reliability

**Zero athletes in the entire 99 have a second test.** So test-retest reliability cannot be estimated from this dataset at all.

That matters because of v1's own finding: a ~3 SD range across 9 categories appears *by chance*. An athlete's highest and lowest categories may be noise. Without a standard error of measurement, you cannot tell a stable trait peak from a bad day — and handing a coach an individual profile built on that would repeat precisely the error v1 caught.

**The fix is cheap and specific: ask S2 for test-retest reliability or SEM per subtest.** With it you compute a reliable-change threshold — the minimum gap between two of an athlete's categories that exceeds measurement error. That converts "his top category is improvisation" into "his improvisation is *reliably* above his decision complexity," which is a defensible coaching statement. Failing that, retest 10–15 athletes and estimate it yourself.

This is worth doing, because it's the analysis that actually delivers your original goal — individualized coaching cues, the option you called the near neighbor in round 1. It just can't be done honestly yet.

## Two housekeeping items

**Three reports beyond the invalid one failed to parse** (Sullivan_Riley, Williams_Palmer, mueller_bronson) — 95 of 99 extracted. The extractor needs hardening before any team-wide run.

**The harvest didn't finish.** It was interrupted after reading the vault conventions — no ledger entry was appended and no articles written. Also worth flagging: `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.json` still points at pre-migration Windows paths (`C:\Users\eric_rash\...`), so any skill trusting it will fail.

Want me to finish the harvest first, or scope the pooled v2 as a proper phase? I'd finish the harvest — the threshold-calibration lesson is the durable asset here, and it applies directly to your ForcePlate and Risk_Stratification work.

# You Cannot Verify a Refactor You Cannot Diff

> **Harvested from:** Kinexon volleyball post-practice report (shipped 2026-08-03)
> **In one sentence:** Make generated artifacts byte-reproducible *before* you need to refactor, because "the output is identical afterwards" is the cheapest and strongest verification available and non-determinism silently takes it away from you.

The job was to extract shared styling and chart code out of a 55 KB file so two
different pages could share one copy. That kind of edit is wide, mechanical, and
exactly where transcription errors hide, so the acceptance test was chosen to be
exact rather than judgemental: generate the page before, extract, generate again,
diff. Identical or the extraction is wrong.

The diff failed — and not because of the extraction. Two builds from *identical
input* were producing different files. The cause was a database query ordered on
only one of its three grouping columns, so a parallel `GROUP BY` returned rows in
a different order on each run, the insertion order of a dictionary followed, and
that ordering rode out into embedded JSON. A one-line fix made three consecutive
builds match exactly, and only then could the refactor be verified at all.

The lesson is the sequencing. Nobody had noticed the non-determinism in months of
use because nothing about the page looked wrong — it was invisible right up until
the moment it blocked the one verification technique that could have made a risky
refactor safe. Reproducibility reads like a nicety when you are producing
artifacts and like a precondition the instant you are changing the code that
produces them.

This applies to anything that emits a file: reports, code generation, fixtures,
exports, snapshot tests, build outputs. The practical rule is to diff two
consecutive builds early, while you have no reason to, and fix whatever differs.
The usual culprits are the ones that feel too small to matter — unordered
queries, hash and set iteration, timestamps, absolute paths, and locale.

## Related

- [[heuristic-suspicion-versus-human-ruling]] — the same project's data-quality lesson
- [[make-generated-claims-score-themselves]] — the same project's lesson on generated prose
- [[standards-without-enforcement]] — a guardrail nobody is held to is decoration; an
  invariant nobody checks is the same failure in code

# A Threshold You Have Not Calibrated Is Not a Threshold

> **Harvested from:** S2 Cognition offensive line review (shipped 2026-08-11)
> **In one sentence:** When a rule fires on the *maximum* across several measures, chance alone will trip it constantly — simulate a population where nothing real is happening and see how often your rule fires there, before you believe a single result it produces.

The rule looked reasonable: flag any athlete sitting 1.5 standard deviations
from his position group on any one of nine cognitive categories. Applied to
fifteen offensive linemen it flagged ten. That reads like a discovery until you
ask what a room containing *no* unusual athlete would have produced. Simulated
with the same fifteen players, the same nine categories and the same observed
spread, the answer was 69% — a central range of seven to thirteen. The observed
ten sat in the middle of pure noise.

The mechanism is that a maximum over many measures is not distributed like any
one of them. Nine independent categories produce an expected spread of roughly
three standard deviations between an athlete's highest and lowest score *with no
underlying profile at all*, so "he is uneven" and "he is far from the group on
something" are the null expectation rather than evidence against it. The same
project had already been bitten by this once, in a gate designed to test whether
a composite score hid useful variation: 89% of purely random athletes would have
passed it. Both times the fix was the same — build the null, count how often the
rule fires there, and only then decide what number means anything.

The tell is any rule of the form *flag if any of these N measures exceeds X*.
Force plate asymmetry across a metric panel, GPS flags across load variables,
wellness questionnaires across subscales, lab panels, any red-amber-green
dashboard that scans several columns and lights up on the worst one. Every added
measure raises the false-positive rate, and the threshold that felt strict when
you were thinking about one variable is permissive across nine.

The practical procedure costs about twenty lines of code: generate a few thousand
synthetic cohorts matching your real n, your number of measures and your observed
spread, containing no real effect by construction; run your rule; report the flag
rate. If your observed rate falls inside that range you have learned nothing, and
should say so rather than publish the names. Do this *before* the data arrives,
because afterwards it is indistinguishable from moving the goalposts.

- [[buchheit-undated-data-everywhere-insight-nowhere-a-practical-quadrant-based-model-for-monitoring-training-l]] — more measures is not more insight

# When You Are Your Own Reviewer, Timestamp the Threshold

> **Harvested from:** S2 Cognition offensive line review (shipped 2026-08-11)
> **In one sentence:** Self-initiated analysis has no outside check, so commit the decision rules to version control *before* obtaining the data — a timestamped commit turns "I set that threshold in advance" from a claim into a fact anyone can verify.

The project was self-initiated, and the person who would judge whether the
finding was interesting was the same person running the analysis. That is the
exact condition under which thresholds drift: not through dishonesty, but
because every number looks negotiable once you can see what it would exclude.
The response was to write the kill criterion, the minimum group size and the
flagging threshold into decision records and commit them to git three days
before the data was obtained, with no data files anywhere in the repository.

It earned its keep almost immediately. Reading the schema revealed the original
criterion was vacuous, and it was replaced — but as a new, reasoned record
explaining why, committed before extraction rather than as a quiet edit to the
old one. Then the flagging threshold produced ten flags from fifteen athletes,
and the calibration showed those flags were noise. The temptation at that moment
is enormous: nudge the number, get a shorter list, ship something interesting.
Because the rule was already timestamped, the only honest moves left were to
report what it gave and report that it was miscalibrated. The result was a null
finding, published — which the original decision record had explicitly named as
a legitimate outcome, precisely so that this moment would not feel like failure.

The generalisable machinery is small. Write the rules down as prose with
reasoning, not as constants buried in a script. Commit before the data exists,
and keep the data out of the repository so the ordering is externally checkable.
When a rule turns out to be wrong, supersede it in a new record that says what
was wrong and why — never edit the original. And commit to publishing the
negative result up front, because a pre-registration you only honour when the
answer is interesting is not one.

This applies well beyond statistics: vendor evaluations where you already prefer
a product, pilot studies you proposed yourself, A/B tests whose result affects
your own roadmap. Anywhere you are both the analyst and the audience, the
timestamp is the only referee available.

# Vendor Percentiles Are Only Comparable Within Their Reference Group

> **Harvested from:** S2 Cognition offensive line review (shipped 2026-08-11)
> **In one sentence:** A percentile is a rank against some specific population, so before comparing athletes on any vendor's percentile scores, find which population each score was ranked against and confirm it is identical for everyone you intend to compare.

A vendor report hands you a number that looks absolute — 86th percentile — and
it is nothing of the kind. It is a rank against a reference group named
somewhere in the report's small print. If that group differs between two
athletes, their percentiles are not on the same scale and any comparison between
them is meaningless, no matter how confident the arithmetic downstream looks.

This nearly broke an analysis built entirely on comparing linemen to each other.
Had the vendor normed each athlete against his own position, every position
group would have been centred near the 50th percentile by construction, and
"deviation from the room" would have been measuring something already removed
before the data arrived. Checking took one pass over the file set to extract a
single line from each report, and it settled the question — the reference group
was identical for every athlete in the room. The same pass caught something
else worth knowing: report *templates* did not always match the folder an
athlete was filed under, so several players carried a different position's
narrative than their room implied.

There is a satisfying empirical test when the documentation is ambiguous, and it
needs no cooperation from the vendor. Compute each group's mean percentile. If
the norming is within-group, every group is pinned near the 50th by definition.
If the groups spread out — in this dataset they ranged from the 42nd to the 82nd
— the norm is common across them and cross-group comparison is legitimate. That
same spread is then interpretable in its own right, though carefully: a group
sitting low against an all-comers norm may say more about what the instrument
measures than about that group's quality.

The check belongs in the intake routine for any normative athlete data —
force plates, GPS benchmarks, cognitive testing, movement screens, physiological
norms. Ask three questions before the first comparison: what population is this
ranked against, is it the same population for every athlete in my dataset, and
did it change between test dates. The third matters because vendors revise
normative databases quietly, and a percentile from 2022 may not sit on the same
scale as one from 2026 even for the same athlete.

cat > docs/V2-SCOPE.md <<'MD'
# V2 Scope — S2 Cognition

**Status:** proposed, not started. V1 shipped 2026-08-11 (null finding, OL room).
**Read first:** `CONTEXT.md` (glossary) and `docs/adr/0001`–`0013`. V2 inherits
every one of them.

---

## Settled in V1 — do not relitigate

Profile Unevenness gates, Room Deviation delivers (0003). Spread computed in
z-space (0004). Per-category deviation, not Mahalanobis (0006). Flag, don't
filter, on selection attributes (0005, 0011). Vendor-invalidated reports
excluded and surfaced for retest (0012).

**The standing rule from 0013:** any threshold whose statistic is a maximum or
range across several measures must be calibrated against a null *before* use.
This bit the project twice. It is not optional in V2.

---

## Five facts that reshape the design

1. **Pooling is valid — verified, not assumed.** If S2 normed within position,
   every room would sit near the 50th percentile. They do not: room composite
   means run from the 42nd (OL) to the 82nd (P/K), team mean 59th. The reference
   group is common across positions, so all athletes share one scale.

2. **Room-by-room does not scale.** Only 3 of 12 rooms clear the n>=10 floor
   (OL 15, WR 13, ILB 10). The other nine hold 5–9 athletes. Twelve rooms times
   nine categories is 108 comparisons — the same trap, larger.

3. **Zero athletes have a second test**, across all 99 reports. Test-retest
   reliability cannot be estimated from this dataset at any n.

4. **The speed/accuracy secondary measures were never used.** They extract
   cleanly from 96 of 99 reports and are arguably more coachable than the nine
   categories: "fast but inaccurate under pressure" is a sentence a position
   coach can act on.

5. **Punters and kickers run a reduced battery.** Three P/K-template reports
   yield 7 values with zero N/A — a structurally different category set, not a
   parse failure. They cannot join a nine-category pooled model.

---

## Three tracks

### Track A — Pooled, position-adjusted analysis  *(unblocked)*

Model each athlete's expected profile from position across all ~92 comparable
athletes, then examine residuals. Two gains over V1: position offsets and
residual spread are estimated from ~92 athletes rather than from a room mean
built on 8–15, and the nine small rooms become analysable instead of excluded.

Add the speed/accuracy measures as a tenth and eleventh dimension.

**Honest expected value.** V1 found the OL room *less* extreme than chance, so
this will probably return nulls too. That is still worth having: a defensible
"all 92 athletes were checked with a calibrated method and no one is an outlier"
closes the question permanently instead of leaving it to be re-asked every
testing cycle. It is cheap now that the machinery exists.

### Track B — Individual reliable-change profiles  *(blocked)*

The analysis that actually delivers the original goal: individualised coaching
cues. Not "is he unusual" but "is his improvisation *reliably* above his decision
complexity" — a within-athlete statement needing no comparison to anyone.

**Blocked on the standard error of measurement.** V1 established that a ~3 SD
range across nine categories arises by chance, so without SEM an athlete's peak
category is indistinguishable from a good day. Building this without reliability
would repeat exactly the error V1 caught.

### Track C — Is the position gradient real?  *(blocked)*

The 42nd-to-82nd spread runs skill-positions-high, big-men-low. That is far more
likely a property of measuring visual and decision speed against an all-comers
norm than a fact about Baylor. Separating the two needs S2's positional norms.

---

## Recommendation: the next action is an email, not an analysis

Both blocked tracks unblock from one request to S2:

1. **Test-retest reliability / SEM for each of the nine categories** (and the
   secondary measures), so within-athlete differences can be given a
   reliable-change threshold.
2. **Positional normative data** — do offensive linemen score lower than
   defensive backs in their reference population generally?
3. Confirmation of what the P/K battery measures and why it differs.
4. Whether the normative database was revised between 2022 and 2026 — five
   athletes tested before this year, and a quietly revised norm would put their
   percentiles on a different scale.

Item 4 matters regardless of which track runs, and V1 could not check it.

If S2 will not supply reliability, retesting 12–15 athletes yields an in-house
estimate and is the cheaper path to Track B.

---

## Decisions needed before V2 starts

- **Run Track A now, or wait for the S2 reply and do A and B together?**
  Recommendation: send the email today, start Track A while waiting. A is
  self-contained and its machinery is reused by B.
- **Does a null Track A result get published like V1's?** Recommendation: yes,
  same pre-commitment, same reasoning.
- **Include P/K on the reduced battery as a separate small analysis, or drop
  them from V2?** Recommendation: drop from the pooled model, note the exclusion.

## Carried forward unchanged

Shape only, no prescription (0002) until a coach is in the room. Sports science
internal remains tier 1. Any new threshold is null-calibrated and committed
before the data is touched. Athlete-level data stays out of version control and
off any published page.

content.text:
Not just normative data — and the one you'd most regret omitting is a different ask entirely.

## The five asks, in priority order

**1. Test-retest reliability or SEM, per category.** This is the big one. It's what unblocks the individual profiles you actually wanted. Ask for the ICC or test-retest correlation *and* the standard error of measurement for each of the 9 categories plus the speed/accuracy measures — ideally over a realistic interval (weeks to months) in a comparable population. Without it you cannot say a player's improvisation is genuinely above his decision complexity rather than a good day on one task.

**2. Was the normative database revised between 2022 and 2026?** This one threatens work already done. Five of your linemen tested before this year. If S2 re-based their norms in between, those percentiles aren't on the same scale as the 2026 cohort, and the room mean V1 computed is partly an artifact. Cheap question, potentially expensive answer.

**3. Positional norms within the reference population.** Do offensive linemen score lower than defensive backs generally? Without this you cannot tell whether your 42nd-percentile OL room is a Baylor fact or a property of the instrument.

**4. What exactly is "NFL PROSPECTS — ALL POSITIONS"?** How many athletes, from which years, selected how. See below — this changes the reading of every number you have.

**5. Why does the P/K battery have 7 measures instead of 9?** Which are omitted, and why. Determines whether kickers can be partially pooled or must stay separate.

## One thing worth knowing before you send

Your reference group is **NFL prospects** — a heavily selected elite population, not college players. That reframes things. Your team mean sits at the **59th percentile of NFL prospects**, and only two rooms fall below the 50th. Read plainly, your athletes are testing above the median NFL prospect on these measures.

V1 never surfaced this because it was scoped to one room and hunting for outliers. It's arguably the most presentable thing in the dataset — and it's exactly why ask #4 matters, because the claim is only as good as the composition of that norm.

## While you wait

**Run the research track first — it may answer ask #1 without S2.** The original routing brief recommended `/research` on S2's construct validity in parallel with the grilling, and it never ran. S2 has published on draft prediction, so reliability coefficients may already exist in the literature. If they do, Track B unblocks immediately and you stop waiting on an email.

**Then Track A prep**, which needs nothing from S2: harden the extractor for the P/K layout and the invalid report, add the speed/accuracy dimensions, and — per the standing rule from ADR 0013 — pre-register and commit Track A's thresholds *before* running it. Same discipline, same reason.

**Contingency worth deciding now:** if S2 won't share reliability, retesting 12–15 athletes gives you an in-house estimate. Fall camp may be the practical window, which makes it a scheduling question rather than an analysis one.

Want me to draft the email to S2, or kick off the research track? I'd do both — the email is short, and the research can run while you send it.

from email.message import EmailMessage
import base64, json

BODY = """Hi [contact],

I'm the sports scientist with Baylor Athletics Applied Performance. We've been
using S2 Cognition with our football roster, and I'm running some internal
analysis across our position groups. There are a few things I can't determine
from the reports themselves. If any of this is already documented, a pointer is
all I need.

1) Test-retest reliability / standard error of measurement

For each of the nine skill categories, and for the speed and accuracy secondary
measures, do you have test-retest reliability coefficients and/or SEM values
from a comparable population and interval? I want to know how large a
difference between two of an athlete's own categories has to be before it
exceeds measurement error. Without that I don't think it's responsible to put an
individual profile in front of a position coach.

2) Revisions to the normative database

Our reports span July 2022 through July 2026. Has the reference database been
re-based at any point in that window? If it has, percentiles from different
years wouldn't sit on the same scale, which affects whether we can compare
athletes tested in different years.

3) Composition of the reference group

Our reports are scored against "NFL PROSPECTS - ALL POSITIONS." Roughly how many
athletes does that comprise, from which years, and how were they selected? It
matters for how we describe a given percentile internally.

4) Positional differences within the reference population

Do scores differ systematically by position among NFL prospects - for example,
do offensive linemen differ from defensive backs on these measures generally?
This determines whether a position group's average is telling us something about
our athletes or about the instrument.

5) Punter and kicker battery

Our P/K reports return seven measures rather than nine. Which are omitted, and
what's the reasoning?

Anything you can share, published or internal, would be genuinely useful. Happy
to set up a call if that's easier than writing it out.

Thanks,
Eric Rash
Applied Performance - Baylor Athletics
"""

m = EmailMessage()
m["Subject"] = "S2 Cognition - request for reliability and reference group documentation"
m["To"] = ""
m.set_content(BODY)
raw = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(m.as_bytes()).decode()
json.dump({"message": {"raw": raw}}, open("draft.json", "w"))
print(f"built: subject set, body {len(BODY)} chars, raw {len(raw)} b64 chars, To left blank")

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. **Primary Request and Intent:**

   The user (Eric Rash, `eric.rash11@gmail.com`, Baylor Athletics Applied Performance) asked, across a sequence of requests:
   - Start a new `/project` titled "S2 evaluation", create a folder in the DEV root, and use `/ask-matt` to decide the best workflow.
   - Proceed with grilling (design interview) despite not yet having the data on-machine and not having run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.
   - Run `/mattpocock-skills:handoff` (twice; second time with args "to contiue project in a new window").
   - Take the handoff and continue; PDF reports are at `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/COG_S2_Position_Reports`.
   - Decide D1 (cohort) and D2 (kill-criterion threshold), write the ADR, then "resume".
   - Run `/Harvest`, then later "finish the harvest".
   - Answer whether the project can scale to the rest of the team and whether an individual-athlete secondary analysis is possible.
   - "Go ahead and push, commit, and then scope for V2."
   - "You're approved to launch the private Git repo."
   - "Draft the email but use the gws-cli to put it in drafts of my gmail."
   - "compact"

   Core project intent: mine existing S2 Cognition testing data for actionable, coach-facing insight that goes **beyond normative percentiles**. Session renamed to `S2_Cognition_Insights`, color orange.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **Profile Unevenness** (within-athlete spread across categories) vs **Room Deviation** (distance from position-group mean) — separating these was the hardest-won design result
   - Pre-registration of thresholds in timestamped git commits before data acquisition
   - Null-model calibration of thresholds; max-over-N inflation (multiple comparisons)
   - z-space arithmetic via inverse normal (`scipy.stats.norm.ppf`) with reporting back in percentile language
   - Bonferroni correction; ICC / SEM / reliable change index
   - ADR (Architecture Decision Record) + CONTEXT.md glossary discipline (`/domain-modeling`)
   - Matt Pocock skill flow: `/grill-with-docs` → `/research` → `/prototype` → `/to-spec` → `/to-tickets` → `/implement`
   - `dataviz` skill procedure: form → color → **script validation** → marks → hover → a11y → render-and-look
   - Artifact three-state theming (`:root`, `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded with `:root:not([data-theme="light"])`, `:root[data-theme="dark"]`)
   - `gws` Google Workspace CLI, Gmail Drafts API, RFC822 + base64url
   - `uv run --with <pkg>` for ephemeral Python deps (never global pip, per CLAUDE.md)

3. **Files and Code Sections:**

   - **`/Users/kristinarash/DEV/S2_Evaluation/CONTEXT.md`** — glossary, 8 terms, conforms to `CONTEXT-FORMAT.md` (term + 1-2 sentences + `_Avoid_`). Terms: Beyond Percentiles, Profile Shape, Profile Unevenness, Room Deviation, Position Fit (resolved to fit-*within*-position), Room, Vendor Baseline, Kill Criterion.

   - **`docs/adr/0001`–`0013`** — the decision record. Key ones:
     - 0001 pre-registered kill criterion (threshold pending schema)
     - 0002 v1 scope: one-off, single room, internal audience, **shape only, no prescription**
     - 0003 Unevenness gates, Room Deviation delivers; OL chosen over safeties on room-size grounds
     - 0004 compute spread in z-space (population SD = 1, so room SD never estimated)
     - 0005 cohort: include everyone with data, flag don't filter; most recent test
     - 0006 per-category deviation + max-abs ranking; **rejected Mahalanobis** (small-n covariance)
     - 0007 room floor n ≥ 10, else combined big-men room
     - 0008 flag at 1.5 SD absolute, **rejected top-N**
     - 0009 go/no-go is self-assessed (this is *why* pre-registration is load-bearing)
     - 0010 kill criterion replaced: **mean category range ≥ 2.5 SD** vs null (2.97 independent / 2.10 r≈0.5 / 1.33 r≈0.8)
     - 0011 include all 16 across mixed test years, flag year as diagnostic
     - 0012 exclude the one vendor-INVALID report; surface as retest recommendation
     - 0013 flagging threshold was uncalibrated; **finding is null**; thresholds must be null-calibrated before use

   - **`docs/WORKFLOW.md`** — ask-matt routing brief. Contains the "Robertson et al. 2017" citation that produced the `roberts` false positive in the PII audit.

   - **`docs/V2-SCOPE.md`** (119 lines, commit `77355dc`) — five facts reshaping design; three tracks (A pooled/unblocked, B individual/blocked on SEM, C position gradient/blocked); recommendation that the next action is an email not an analysis.

   - **`build_report.py`** — generates `report.html` from `data/ol_scores.csv` so numbers can't drift. Key CSS pattern:
     ```
     :root{{--bg:#f9f9f7;--surf:#fcfcfb;--ink:#0b0b0b;...--s1:#2a78d6;--s2:#eb6834;}}
     @media (prefers-color-scheme:dark){{:root:not([data-theme="light"]){{...}}}}
     :root[data-theme="dark"]{{...}}
     code,.val,td{{font-family:ui-monospace,...;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}}
     @media (prefers-reduced-motion:reduce){{*{{transition:none!important;...}}}}
     ```
     Bar path helper rounds only the data-end:
     ```python
     def bar(x0,x1,y,h,r=4):
         d=1 if x1>=x0 else -1; r=min(r,abs(x1-x0))
         if r<=0: return f'M{x0},{y}H{x1}V{y+h}H{x0}Z'
         return (f'M{x0},{y}H{x1-d*r}Q{x1},{y} {x1},{y+r}V{y+h-r}Q{x1},{y+h} {x1-d*r},{y+h}H{x0}Z')
     ```

   - **`report.html`** (~16 KB) — de-identified. Published at `https://claude.ai/code/artifact/30d83487-f660-42d7-9810-408f8b622524`.

   - **`.gitignore`** — `.DS_Store`, `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `data/`

   - **`data/ol_scores.csv`, `data/team_scores.csv`** — GITIGNORED, contain athlete PII, never committed.

4. **Errors and fixes:**

Tried `.claude/settings.json` `{"worktree":{"bgIsolation":"none"}}` (settings load at session start, no effect); removed `.git` (still blocked — stale session state). **Fix: write all files via Bash heredocs.** This persisted for the rest of the session.
   - **Artifact 409 conflict** on the portfolio dashboard. Fix: WebFetch the live version, diff project names to prove local was a strict superset (19 vs 20, only delta = S2_Evaluation), then `force:true`.
   - **`$TMPDIR` handoff file swept** within 2 days. Fix: rewrote it and added a self-describing "this document is disposable" note.
   - **Original kill criterion was vacuous** — 89% of pure-noise athletes pass 2.0 SD with 9 categories. Fix: ADR 0010, mean-range-vs-null at 2.5 SD. Caught *before* data.
   - **Flagging threshold uncalibrated** — 10/15 flagged, but null gives 69% (range 7-13). Fix: ADR 0013 records the null finding; **threshold was NOT retuned**.
   - **Gridlines drawn over bars** in chart 2. Fix: moved grid emission before the bar loop.
   - **`artifact-design` skill loaded after writing the page** (should be before). Fix: loaded it, then added mono type role + `prefers-reduced-motion`; then narrowed mono to data cells when it made headers/`≥ 2.5 SD` too wide.
   - **zsh glob expansion on `?`** in `gh api "repos/.../trees/main?recursive=1"` produced "no matches found" and a **FALSE PASS** on the PII leak check. Fix: quoted the URL and re-ran; real result = 19 files, no data paths. (Matches the stored `project_zsh-shell-traps` memory.)
   - **`roberts` PII hit** in git history → false positive, substring of "Robertson et al. 2017". Fix: word-boundary rescan returned NONE.
   - **`gws-cli` doesn't exist** — binary is `gws` at `/opt/homebrew/bin/gws`; no `+draft` helper, so used raw `gws gmail users drafts create`.
   - **`config.json` has stale Windows paths** (`C:\Users\eric_rash\...`) — flagged twice, still unfixed.

5. **Problem Solving:**

   The central achievement: the pre-registration caught a real error in the act. Applied literally, the 1.5 SD rule flagged 10 of 15 linemen — which would have produced a list of "cognitively atypical" players built on nothing. Null calibration showed a homogeneous room flags 7-13 of 15. **The finding is null: no lineman is atypical**, and at 2.5 SD the room produced zero flags where chance predicts 1-2. The threshold was reported as-is with its miscalibration documented rather than retuned.

   Also solved: verified cross-position pooling is legitimate (rooms range 42nd-82nd; if position-normed all would sit at ~50th); identified the P/K reduced battery (7 measures, zero N/A) as structural not a parse bug; audited every blob in git history before creating a remote.

name: domain-modeling
description: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
---

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline — challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill — that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── CONTEXT.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily — only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y — which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account' — do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"

### Update CONTEXT.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up — capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

# S2_Evaluation — recommended workflow

**Project:** Mine existing S2 Cognition testing data for actionable, coach-facing
insights that go beyond normative percentiles.
**Lane:** side · **Stage:** idea · **Registered:** 2026-08-08
**Routed via:** `/ask-matt` (router doc at `~/.agents/skills/ask-matt/SKILL.md`)

---

## The framing problem to solve first

The request as stated — "mine the data for insights" — is open-ended exploration
with no decision anchor. That is the single biggest risk to this project, and your
own material already says so:

- **EOY Kitman Utilization (2026-06-08)**, logged under *Decisions*: "Collecting
  data without a clear plan often leads to unutilized information, reducing
  effective injury prevention."
- **JFrazier Presentation Brief (2026-06-12)**, logged under *Decisions* as a
  "Decision-First Data Approach": "Collect data only after defining specific RTP
  questions to simplify and speed up analysis."
- Robertson et al. 2017 in your library argues athlete monitoring fails without
  *decision-support systems* — more numbers is not the fix.

You have already decided this twice, in writing, in two separate meetings. This
project should not be the exception.

"Beyond percentiles" is a real goal, but an insight that isn't tied to a decision a
coach actually makes is just a prettier percentile. **Step 1 is framing, not
analysis.**

Concretely, the grilling should force answers to: *which coaching decisions should
an S2 insight change?* Candidates worth pressuring — install/rep allocation,
position fit, communication load in complex packages, individualized coaching cues,
pre-snap processing under time pressure. Pick the few that a coach would act on.

---

## Recommended path

### 0. Precondition (gate, not a step)
`/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configures the issue tracker, triage labels, and doc
layout the later steps assume. **No Matt tracker config was found on this machine.**
It is not needed for steps 1–3. Run it only if you reach step 4 (`/to-tickets`).

### 1. `/grill-with-docs` — sharpen the idea, statefully
Run this in `S2_Evaluation/`. Purpose: nail the decision-first frame above, and
build the glossary.

Strictly, `/ask-matt` routes an empty folder to `/grill-me` (no codebase). Use
`/grill-with-docs` anyway — `/grill-me` is **stateless and saves nothing**, and
this project will accumulate decisions worth a paper trail (`CONTEXT.md` + ADRs).
Precedent: `SportScienceResearchRepo`, `ZoteroInjestion`, and `PlayerProfiles_FB`
all carry a `CONTEXT.md` from this flow.

Expect `/domain-modeling` to get pulled in underneath: **"S2 score" is an
overloaded term** doing at least four jobs — raw subtest value, subtest percentile,
composite, and normative-population percentile. Resolving that is a prerequisite to
saying anything precise about "beyond percentiles."

### 2. `/research` — run in the background, in parallel with step 1
Delegate to a background agent, against **primary sources**: what each S2 subtest
actually claims to measure, and the published evidence on predictive validity for
on-field performance. It leaves a cited Markdown file in the repo.

This is not optional politeness. If you mine a pattern that contradicts the
instrument's known construct validity, you will present it to a coach and be wrong.
Pair with your own `sports-science-research-grounding` and
`pp-zotero-research-library` skills.

### 3. `/prototype` — answer "is there signal?" with throwaway code
The question *"is there anything beyond percentiles in this data?"* cannot be
settled on paper. It needs a runnable answer, which is exactly the step-2 detour in
the main flow.

`/prototype` fits exploratory data analysis almost perfectly: **throwaway from day
one — keep the answer, delete the code.** Probe intra-athlete profile *shape*
(strength/weakness dispersion, not rank), change across testing cycles,
position-relevant subtest weighting, and subtest interactions.

Bridge with `/handoff` in both directions — out of the grilling session into a
fresh prototype session, then back with what you learned.

### 4. Branch — only after step 3 finds signal
- **Multi-session build** (likely, if this becomes a recurring per-testing-cycle
  deliverable) → `/to-spec`, then `/to-tickets`, then `/implement` per ticket,
  **clearing context between each one**.
- **Small enough** → `/implement` directly.

`/implement` drives `/tdd` internally and closes with `/code-review` before
committing.

**Context hygiene:** keep steps 1–4 through `/to-tickets` in one unbroken context
window. If you approach the smart zone (~120k tokens) first, `/handoff` rather than
push on degraded.

---

## The last mile `/ask-matt` does not cover

`/ask-matt` routes **engineering** work. Your actual deliverable is **coach-facing**,
which is a data-storytelling problem, not a code problem. Once you have findings:

- **`design-academy-skill`** — audience-first data storytelling; it triggers exactly
  on "showing data to an audience."
- **`dataviz`** — read *before* writing the first line of chart code.
- **`five-slides-generator`** — if the output should land in the Performance School
  "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" format.

---

## Explicitly not recommended

- **`/triage`** — only for issues *you didn't create*. Nothing inbound here.
- **`/diagnosing-bugs`** — nothing is broken.
- **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** — no codebase yet.
- **`/wayfinder`** — the escalation, not the start. It charts investigation tickets
  for efforts too big for one session. Reach for it only if step 1 reveals the fog
  is deeper than a single grilling session; with data already in hand, grill +
  prototype is right-sized for a side-lane project.

---

## Immediate next action

Run `/grill-with-docs` in `S2_Evaluation/` to fix the decision-first frame — name
the specific coaching decisions an S2 insight should change, before touching the
data. Kick off `/research` in the background at the same time.

**Still unknown:** where the S2 Cognition data actually lives, its format, athlete
count, and how many testing cycles deep it goes. The grilling should surface this
early — it bounds what step 3 can attempt.

# /project — portfolio registry skill

Drives the shipped `project-triage` CLI to capture ideas, log progress, and
keep the front-burner dashboard current. The registry (`portfolio.json`) is
the single source of truth — never hand-edit `dashboard.html`.

## Paths

- Repo: `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage`
- Interpreter: `python3`
- Registry: `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/portfolio.json`
- CLI entry points: `portfolio.py` (mutations), `render.py` (render)
- Generated: `dashboard.html`, `pulse.md` (both written next to the scripts;
  do not edit by hand, they are regenerated every render)

## CLI contract (verbatim — do not alter flags)

```
& "python3" "/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/portfolio.py" add-idea "<pitch>" --source "<source>"
& "python3" "/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/portfolio.py" add-update "<name>" "<note>" --next-action "<optional>"
& "python3" "/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/portfolio.py" set-stage "<name>" "<stage>"
& "python3" "/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/render.py"
& "python3" "/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/render.py" --no-scan
```

- `add-idea` prints `idea captured (<N> in inbox)`.
- `add-update` prints `updated <name>` (name match is case-insensitive).
- `set-stage` prints `stage set: <name> → <stage>`. Valid stages, in ladder
  order: `idea grilled spec planned building shipped`.
- `render.py` (full scan) prints `wrote dashboard.html · wrote pulse.md · ...`.
- `render.py --no-scan` does the same but skips the DEV/ activity heuristics
  (fast; use it after any registry mutation, and to validate hand-edits).
- Any error path prints `[error] <msg>` to stderr and exits 2, with no
  mutation to `portfolio.json`. Stop and surface the message verbatim.

## Verbs

### `idea <pitch>`
Run `add-idea "<pitch>" --source "<conversation context, ≤8 words>"`. The
source should summarize where the idea came from (e.g. "chat about GPS
vendor gaps"), not just "chat". Then do the render + republish ritual.

### `update <name> <note>`
Fuzzy-match `<name>` against the project names currently in the registry
(read `portfolio.json` first). If exactly one match, run `add-update "<name>"
"<note>"` (add `--next-action "<...>"` if the user gave one). If the match is
ambiguous or there's no close match, ask the user which project they mean
before running anything. Then do the render + republish ritual.

### `rank`
Read `portfolio.json`, show both lanes' active projects with their current
`rank` values, and ask for the new order. Never reorder ranks yourself —
only apply the order the user gives you. Rewrite the `rank` fields directly
with the Edit tool, then validate by running `render.py --no-scan` (exit 0
means the edit is structurally valid). Then do the render + republish
ritual (this counts as the render step — no need to run render.py twice).

### `promote <idea>`
Ask which lane (`job` or `side`) and for a `next_action`. With the Edit
tool: set the matching idea's `status` to `promoted`, and append a new
project entry to that lane at the next free `rank` (max existing rank in
that lane + 1). Validate with `render.py --no-scan`, then do the render +
republish ritual.

### `stage <name> <stage>`
Fuzzy-match `<name>` like `update` does. Run `set-stage "<name>" "<stage>"`.
The dashboard auto-detects spec/plan docs (in the project's DEV folder under
`docs/specs`, `docs/plans`, or the `docs/superpowers/...` variants) and
renders plan-checkbox progress — the stage is your curated claim; drift
between the two shows on the card. Then do the render + republish ritual.

**Shipped → harvest handoff:** when the stage being set is `shipped`, after
the ritual offer once: "Want me to run /harvest on <name> to distill it into
your SecondBrain and log the shipped artifact?" On yes, invoke the `harvest`
skill for that project.

### bare `/project`
Do the render + republish ritual, then show the contents of `pulse.md` in
chat.

## Render + republish ritual (run after every mutation)

1. Run `render.py --no-scan` (fast path — the mutation verbs above already
   changed the registry; a full DEV/ scan isn't needed unless the user
   explicitly asks for a fresh scan).
2. Read `meta.artifact_url` from `portfolio.json`.
   - If non-empty: publish `dashboard.html` via the Artifact tool passing
     `url: <meta.artifact_url>`, `favicon: "🔥"`, `title: "Portfolio — Front
     Burner"`.
   - If empty: publish `dashboard.html` via the Artifact tool with
     `favicon: "🔥"`, `title: "Portfolio — Front Burner"` (no `url`). Take
     the returned URL, write it into `meta.artifact_url` with the Edit tool,
     then re-run `render.py --no-scan` and republish once more (now with
     `url` set) so the rendered page displays its own share URL.

## Rules

- Never reorder project ranks yourself — only apply the order the user
  gives you during `rank`.
- Never delete a project or idea without explicit confirmation.
- On any `[error] ...` output from the CLI: stop immediately, show the
  error verbatim, and do not proceed to render/publish.
- `portfolio.json` is the single source of truth. Never edit
  `dashboard.html` directly — it is fully regenerated by `render.py`.

# Ask Matt

You don't remember every skill, so ask.

A **flow** is a path through the skills. Most paths run along one **main flow**, and two **on-ramps** merge onto it. Everything else is standalone, or a vocabulary layer that runs underneath.

## The main flow: idea → ship

The route most work travels. You have an idea and want it built.

1. **`/grill-with-docs`** — sharpen the idea by interview. Start here when you **have a codebase**: it's stateful, retaining what it learns in `CONTEXT.md` and ADRs. (No codebase? Use `/grill-me` — see Standalone. Both run the same `/grilling` primitive; `grill-with-docs` is the one that leaves a paper trail.)
2. **Branch — can you settle every question in conversation?** If a question needs a runnable answer (state, business logic, a UI you have to see), detour through a prototype, bridged by **`/handoff`** in both directions (see Crossing sessions):
   - **`/handoff`** out, then open a fresh session against that file,
   - **`/prototype`** to answer the question with throwaway code,
   - **`/handoff`** back what you learned, and reference it from the original idea thread.
3. **Branch — is this a multi-session build?**
   - **Yes** → **`/to-spec`** (turn the thread into a spec), then **`/to-tickets`** to split it into tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its **blocking edges**. On a local tracker that's an ordered `tickets.md` you work by hand; on a real tracker the edges become native blocking links, so any ticket whose blockers are done can be grabbed — kick off **`/implement`** per ticket, **clearing context between each one**.
   - **No** → **`/implement`** right here, in the same context window.

   Either way, **`/implement`** builds each issue by driving **`/tdd`** internally — one red-green slice at a time — then closes out by running **`/code-review`**, a two-axis review (Standards + Spec) of the diff, before committing. Reach for **`/tdd`** on its own when you just want to build a concrete behaviour test-first without a full spec, and **`/code-review`** on its own whenever you want to review a branch or PR against a fixed point.

### Context hygiene

Keep steps 1–3 in **one unbroken context window** — don't compact or clear until after `/to-tickets` — so the grilling, spec, and tickets all build on the same thinking. Each `/implement` then starts fresh, working from the ticket.

The limit on this is the **[smart zone](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/smart-zone)**: the window (~120k tokens on state-of-the-art models) within which the model still reasons sharply. If a session approaches it before `/to-tickets`, don't push on degraded — `/handoff` and continue in a fresh thread.

## On-ramps

A starting situation that generates work, then merges onto the main flow.

- **Bugs and requests piling up** → **`/triage`**. It moves issues through triage roles and produces agent-ready issues, which **`/implement`** later picks up.

  Triage is only for issues **you didn't create** — bug reports, incoming feature requests, anything that arrives raw. Tickets that `/to-tickets` produced are already agent-ready, so **don't triage them**.

- **Something's broken** → **`/diagnosing-bugs`**. For the hard ones: the bug that resists a first glance, the intermittent flake, the regression that crept in between two known-good states. It refuses to theorise until it has a **tight feedback loop** — one command that already goes red on *this* bug — then fixes with a regression test. Its post-mortem hands off to **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** when the real finding is that there's no good seam to lock the bug down.

- **A huge, foggy effort — a greenfield project or a huge feature build, too big for one session** → **`/wayfinder`**. When the way from here to the destination isn't visible yet, it charts a **shared map** of investigation tickets on the issue tracker and resolves them one at a time — producing **decisions, not deliverables** — until the fog is pushed back and the way is clear. Then it merges onto the main flow at **`/to-spec`** (or, if the effort turned out small enough, straight to **`/implement`**). Where **`/grill-with-docs`** sharpens an idea you can hold in one session, wayfinder is for the idea you can't.

## Codebase health

Not feature work — upkeep.

- **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** — run whenever you have a spare moment to keep the codebase good for agents to operate in. It surfaces **deepening opportunities**; picking one _generates an idea_ you can take into the main flow at `/grill-with-docs`. It's the survey that finds the candidates; **`/codebase-design`** (below) is the bench you design the chosen one on.

## Vocabulary underneath

Two model-invoked references that run *beneath* the other skills — each the single source of truth for its vocabulary. Reach for them directly when the **words**, not the process, are the problem; or let the skills above pull them in.

- **`/domain-modeling`** — sharpen the project's *domain* language: challenge a fuzzy term, resolve an overloaded word ("account" doing three jobs), record a hard-to-reverse decision as an ADR. It's the active discipline `/grill-with-docs` drives to keep `CONTEXT.md` a clean glossary.
- **`/codebase-design`** — the deep-module vocabulary (module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality) for designing a module's *shape*: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface at a clean seam. `/tdd` and `/improve-codebase-architecture` both speak it.

## Crossing sessions

- **`/handoff`** — when a thread is full or you need to branch off (e.g. into a `/prototype` session), this compacts the conversation into a markdown file. You don't continue in place — you **open a new session and reference that file** to carry the context across. It's the bridge between context windows, in either direction. Use it when you want a **fresh session** but need the **current conversation preserved**.
- **`/compact`** (built-in) — stay in the **same conversation**, letting the earlier turns be summarized. Use it at **intentional breaks between phases**, when you don't mind losing the verbatim history. Don't compact mid-phase — the agent can lose its way. `/handoff` forks; `/compact` continues.

## Standalone

Off the main flow entirely.

- **`/grill-me`** — the same relentless interview as `/grill-with-docs`, but for when you have **no codebase**. Stateless: it saves nothing locally, builds no `CONTEXT.md`. Reach for it to sharpen any plan or design that doesn't live in a repo.
- **`/prototype`** — a small, throwaway program that answers one design question: does this state model feel right, or what should this UI look like. Throwaway from day one — keep the answer, delete the code. It's the detour in step 2 of the main flow, but reach for it any time a design question is hard to settle on paper.
- **`/research`** — delegate reading legwork to a **background agent**: it investigates a question against **primary sources**, then leaves a cited Markdown file in the repo. Keep working while it reads. The file it produces is something to take *into* the main flow at `/grill-with-docs` — research feeds the thinking, it doesn't replace it.
- **`/teach`** — learn a concept over multiple sessions, using the current directory as a stateful workspace.
- **`/writing-great-skills`** — reference for writing and editing skills well.

## Precondition

**`/setup-matt-pocock-skills`** — run before your first engineering flow to configure the issue tracker, triage labels, and doc layout the other skills assume. Custom issue trackers also work.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]
